articles.headline: 'We've moved on' - Martinez in Man Utd squad to face Leeds
keyFacts: Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez is included in the squad to face Leeds United after apologizing for criticizing club hierarchy.
Head coach Michael Carrick stated that the situation is resolved and the team has moved on from the incident.
Martinez previously criticized director Jason Wilcox over transfer investment following a Champions League defeat to Atletico Madrid.
body: Lisandro Martinez: Man Utd defender in squad for Leeds trip as Michael Carrick insists situation resolved

Man Utd boss Michael Carrick insists Lisandro Martinez situation has been resolved and the defender realises "he made a mistake" by criticising the club's hierarchy after Tuesday's defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League
Friday 16 October 2026 14:15, UK
Lisandro Martinez is set to be in Manchester United’s squad for Sunday's trip to Leeds United after he apologised for the public nature of his outburst about the club's hierarchy.

Head coach Michael Carrick insisted the situation has been resolved and that "we have moved on" in a press conference dominated by questions about Martinez after he called out director of football Jason Wilcox over a lack of investment in transfer window.

Martinez, whose outspoken comments came after Tuesday's 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid, met the club's hierarchy, including Wilcox and CEO Omar Berrada, and Carrick, on Thursday before making an apology.
- Lisandro Martinez outburst Q&A: Wilcox, transfer strategy and what next
- 'Awful' and 'disrespectful' - Carra and Rooney criticise Martinez outburst
- Martinez's Man Utd future in doubt after comments
Asked about Martinez on Friday ahead of Sunday's trip to Leeds, live on Sky Sports, Carrick said: "He's released his statement and realised he made a mistake.
"That's enough for us to move on with. From our point of view, the acknowledgement of what's been done is enough to move on."
United legends Wayne Rooney and Gary Neville have criticised Martinez for his comments, questioning what impact it might have on the club's dressing room.
But Carrick, who is under mounting pressure with United on a five-game winless run, was adamant that the spirit of the group remains
"We've moved on from that," said the United boss. "As a group we've moved on. It's really not a drama for the group. The squad have trained really well and they are in good spirits.

"It was pretty simple. We understood the situation. Licha understood he made a mistake. We have a really good felling from the club. Results wise it hasn't gone our way, but the spirit and togetherness. We can see in the group we want to do something with this situation.
"We've moved on. Genuinely. There is a freshness about the group."
Analysis: Carrick handled situation well – but talking needs to be on the pitch
Sky Sports' Pete Gill:
"As a player, Michael Carrick was unflustered and calm.

"In Friday's press conference, he has been no different. He offered a straight bat to the inevitable questions about Martinez and only seem ruffled when it was suggested that he needed a result against Leeds - "we need a result" interjected the United head coach.

"Ultimately, though, United's talking needs to be on the pitch. And if there was one jarring note in the presser, it was Carrick's insistence that all is well at United that stood out. United are not, in his words, "in a good place". They can only be if they arrest their alarming slump in form, starting at Leeds on Sunday."
'Doubts over Martinez future'
Sky Sports News' Football Correspondent Rob Dorsett:
There are real doubts about whether Martinez's contract will be extended when it expires in the summer.
Manchester United will focus on revamping their defence in the next transfer windows and have the formal option to prolong Martinez's stay for a further year.
Sky Sports News has been told United are looking at new centre-backs, as well as left-backs.
It is also understood that there is no pressure on Wilcox internally regarding his position.
Martinez has been keen on a move away from Old Trafford for some time.

In the summer, he pushed for a move to Atletico Madrid, the side that beat United in the Champions League on Tuesday night, to follow his good friend and international team-mate, Cristian Romero, who left Spurs for Spain.
No suitable bid for Martinez came in for Manchester United to consider.
The 28-year-old made similar explosive comments about his bosses when at Ajax in 2022. Martinez, who again wanted a move away, called their sporting director Gerry Hamstra a "nobody".

articles.headline: 'One of the best weeks of my life' - Kartal feeling fresh ahead of Wuhan semi-finals
keyFacts: British tennis player Sonay Kartal reached the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open after beating world No 6 Elina Svitolina.
Kartal said she is enjoying one of the best weeks of her life following an injury-ravaged season.
Kartal will play against Jelena Ostapenko on Saturday in the semi-finals.
body: Sonay Kartal: British star says she is due a couple of new tattoos after reaching Wuhan Open semi-finals

Sonay Kartal is enjoying incredible run in China following injury-ravaged season; British player takes on Jelena Ostapenko on Saturday, live on Sky Sports Tennis from 10am; Kartal says she is enjoying "one of the best weeks" of her life
Friday 16 October 2026 13:47, UK
British star Sonay Kartal says she is due a couple of new tattoos after enjoying "one of the best weeks" of her life by reaching the semi-finals of the Wuhan Open.
Kartal claimed one of the biggest wins of the career as she beat world No 6 Elina Svitolina on Friday.
The 24-year-old, playing in only her third tournament since returning from a back injury, seized her first match-point opportunity to complete another stunning victory.

- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream no contract on NOW
Kartal, who made her breakthrough by reaching the fourth round of last year's Wimbledon, advanced to the last four of a WTA 1000 event for the first time.
"Definitely one of the best weeks of my life," she said. "You could say, results-wise, that is definitely the best for me so far.

"I'm very happy to be backing up the level each day. I think it's pretty easy for a player to come out and play a blinder for just one match. I'm very happy that I managed to keep the consistency. I've got some of my best wins this week."
Kartal added she is due a couple of new tattoos. She had one booked in but was forced to make a last-minute cancellation after heading to the Billie Jean King Cup with Great Britain.
Asked if she would get one done if she won in Wuhan, the Brighton-based star replied with a smile: "I would have to have a think. I can't make a rush decision."
Back injury and protected ranking

Kartal, using a protected injury ranking to play, has previously peaked at No 44 in the rankings and started the Wuhan Open at No 170, but she has skyrocketed 83 places to No 87 in the live rankings with her run to the semi-finals.
She is assured of adding 390 points to her total, meaning she is guaranteed to be the new British No 2 behind Katie Boulter (No 58), moving past Fran Jones (No 98) and Emma Raducanu (No 109).
Having missed more than six months, Kartal admitted she would not be able to walk without some form of pain but found it "pretty smooth sailing" after a couple of months.
And now she is feeling fit and healthy again.
"My back is great," Kartal said. "I wouldn't have made the return if it wasn't great.

"I think the body is feeling it having not played a tennis match for six months, and when you're on tour, your body gets used to the aches and pains and demands of matches each week. I'm definitely more sore in areas.

"I think if there's one thing I've learned in the six months - it's sometimes patience is the better option. And the heroic thing to do is not play every single week. I feel great and I'm ready to get going for the remainder of the year."
The challenge of Ostapenko
She'll next face Latvian world No 34 Jelena Ostapenko, who beat Diana Shnaider in her quarter-final.
The pair have met twice before, with both matches coming on grass in the space of six days in June 2025 - Ostapenko won at Eastbourne, but then Kartal came out on top at Wimbledon.
"I've enjoyed playing her," said Kartal. "I think we're equal on the scoreboard. But I think there's a level of respect that she shows me.
"She's playing great this week having had a few tough matches, so she's definitely on form. I'm excited for another battle.
"I feel it's going to be a completely different game style to the people that I've played the past few days. I'm ready for a long one if it's needed."

body: Can the Green Bay Packers win a third straight game when the Dallas Cowboys come to Lambeau Field for a primetime showdown in Week 6? Of the 54 experts reviewed this week, roughly 70 percent picked the Packers to win straight up. Many of those predicting a final score envisioned a game with a lot of points, which isn't surprising given the quality of the two offenses, especially at quarterback and wide receiver, and the 40-40 tie that took place between the two teams last year. articles.headline: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will reopen if U.S. leaves region
keyFacts: An Iranian army official stated Friday that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the United States leaves the Middle East.
A Norwegian teenager was sentenced in the United Kingdom to 20 years in prison for plotting a murder for an Iran-linked gang.
Sources told CBS News that the White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a large bomb on Iranian military sites if ordered by President Trump.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:
- The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for 's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X.

- Ships remain exposed to , even if they try to hide their movements by switching off tracking systems, a maritime monitor warned Thursday, confirming three strikes on vessels in the waterway this week.

- The launched a strike Thursday on the presidential palace in Yemen's government-held de facto capital of Aden. The attack caused multiple deaths and injuries among the security staff, according to the internationally recognized government.
Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang
A Norwegian teenager convicted of on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.

Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K.

In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall.
It remains unknown who his intended target would have been.

Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit.

Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.
CBS/AP
Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman
The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area."
The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman."

The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels."
At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week.
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region"
The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday.

"If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X. "If it does not leave, we will expel it."

He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel.

Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels, Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission.

Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turned off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection.
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide"
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country.
Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions."

"What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News.

"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
CBS/AFP
White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."

A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.

Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.

articles.headline: Ugly side effects of a 24-team College Football Playoff: The death of best regular season in sports and more
keyFacts: The College Football Playoff is moving toward expanding its field to 24 teams to generate more games and revenue.
A Sporting News poll indicated that 80.7% of surveyed fans oppose the 24-team model.
Critics state that the expansion will reduce regular-season stakes, increase regular-season rematches, and potentially eliminate conference championships.
body: The college football regular season is about to die.
The College Football Playoff is getting closer to expanding the size of the field to 24 teams – a move that doubles the size of the 12-team model.
For college football coaches, athletic directors and television executives, this is a financial move that means more games and more revenue.
For college football fans?

There is no doubt it does not win the popular vote. A Sporting News poll revealed that 80.7% of college football fans are not in favor of the 24-team model. It's a small sample – but we're willing to bet most polls show similar results.
Are you in favor of 24-team College Football Playoff?
— Bill Bender (@BillBender92) October 15, 2026

It's a radical change – and the most talked about side effect is the very reason for its lack of popularity. A 24-team College Football Playoff kills the college football regular season. We're 80.7% sure that's true. How do you sell something eight out of 10 people don't want?
MORE: College Football Playoff forecast ahead of Week 7
Is the CFP better with 24 teams?
A 24-team model guarantees more schools will be involved in the postseason. A total of 80 teams would have participated in the College Football Playoff since 2014 with a 24-team model.
A total of 31 of those schools would have made the playoff four times. Iowa and Oklahoma State – schools that have yet to make the CFP – would have made it six times each.

Would that success be appreciated as much as it is in the 12-team CFP era? The answer is, "Hell, no." No. 12 UCLA and No. 15 Kentucky were darlings of the first half of the college football season – and it’s the possibility of that first playoff appearance that makes it even better. The Bruins and Wildcats would have already had two appearances each in the 24-team model. Will Stein's two-point magic and Bob Chesney's pre-game speeches resonate less.
BENDER: Oklahoma State's Drew Mestemaker continues his improbable rise
David Leong/Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
Does 24-team CFP devalue college football regular season?
College football's regular season, which was the best regular season in sports, is no longer that. Notice we said "was."

Week 6 best illustrates that point. No. 1 Georgia beat No. 6 Alabama 20-17 at Bryant-Denny Stadium. Was the vision test on that game better, worse or the same as San Francisco's 32-29 victory against Seattle in a NFC West showdown the following day?
At best, the answer is "the same." Watching college football feels like watching the NFL, which is great for business. Follow the TV model.

The game between the 49ers-Seahawks averaged 26.697 million viewers in the afternoon window for "America's Game of the Week" on Fox. Georgia-Alabama averaged 12.24 million viewers in prime time on ABC's "Saturday Night Football."
With more playoff teams, our bet is the television numbers decrease in college football for games like that. Why?

Stakes. That's the one thing big college football regular-season games like that used to have on the NFL. As we pointed out last week, there were 14 top-10 showdowns in college football from 2024-25. Both teams made the playoff in six of those games - or 42.9%. That number will increase exponentially in a 24-team playoff. What's the meaning of those games? And yes, Michigan-Ohio State could move from the final week of the regular season to avoid coaches sitting star players before the first week of the CFP.

One could argue back that the 49ers-Seahawks will run that back in the regular season – and in the NFC playoffs. Or that increased field will incentivize better non-conference matchups – which was a glaring issue this September and create better conference races.

It does not prevent re-runs. Rematches have never been met with the same excitement in college football. Georgia-Ole Miss and Alabama-Oklahoma were rematches of regular-season SEC games last year. The 2012 Alabama-LSU rematch in the BCS championship game telegraphed the end of the BCS era.

Why is that? You're watching an NFL-style regular season with players who aren't as good and games that don't mean as much when three- and four-loss teams get in the playoff. If you want a regular season that is more like men's college basketball or MLB, then, well, you get what you wanted.
MORE: Picks for Ohio State-Indiana, BYU-ND and more
Will college football fans adjust to a 24-team CFP?
Will we adjust? It's going to be more difficult this time. That 19.3% who welcome the 24-team College Football Playoff will say so. They're more open-minded, but they're also wrong.

The Bowl Championship Series was a system shock in 1998, and No. 1 Tennessee's 23-16 victory against No. 2 Florida State in the Fiesta Bowl wasn't an overly compelling game. But it came one year after Michigan and Nebraska split a national championship – the third spilt national title of the decade. There has been one split national championship since.

The four-team playoff generated more excitement in 2014, and opened with a banger of a semifinal when No. 4 Ohio State upset No. 1 Alabama in the Sugar Bowl. Unfortunately, that foreshadowed a decade where seven schools – Alabama, Ohio State, Clemson, Oklahoma, Georgia and Michigan – combined for 75% of the appearances.

The 12-team playoff wasn't given enough time to breathe. Ohio State's national title was expected. Indiana's unbeaten season? No way. The on-campus games are a hit – and it offers just enough exclusivity that teams like Notre Dame and Texas paid for regular-season losses last year.

Doubling down on the size of the field means that's over. Get ready to argue about three- and four-loss teams in the SEC and Big Ten. It's going to be more like Bubble Talk during March Madness – and that just is not nearly as fun.
Other side effects of 24-team CFP
The regular season isn't the only notable side effect of a 24-team College Football Playoff. Here are some other immediate impacts that are less severe than the regular season:

Conference championships. Those will be gone. In a 24-team playoff that makes sense, but it begs a question. What's the point of being in a conference outside of revenue? Does this open the door for the Super League?

Role of the Group of 6. A Group of 6 conference school would reportedly be included in the 24-team field. What if they aren't ranked among the top 24 teams? Will this lead to the G6 having their separate playoff down the road?

Bowl games. The nature of Bowl Season will change. Perhaps some bowl games will be moved to the regular season and played as neutral-site games. This isn't a deal-breaker – but the 24-team playoff is a huge victory for the "bowls are meaningless" crowd.

Scheduling. The 24-team College Football Playoff will start two weeks after the end of the regular season. How do you fit 23 postseason games in the calendar and maintain interest while going head to head with the NFL in late December and January? Proponents will say, "More football won't hurt anybody!" Are they right? This year's championship game is Jan. 25, 2027 at Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas.

articles.headline: Developer vibe-codes a free local Office clone for your browser
keyFacts: Developer Paul Ford released Tiny Little Office, a browser-based office suite featuring ten different tools built with AI assistance.
File changes are saved directly into the URL, allowing users to share links that can be password-protected or set to expire.
The open-source project lacks cloud access or real-time collaboration, saving files locally instead.
body: - A new vibe-coded app offers a simple, browser-based office suite
- Each file is 'saved' in the code for the URL
- The apps come with a variety of options for sharing links/files

AI vibe coding is now at the stage where these apps and agents can clone big-name software packages just by observing how they work. Now there's a new web app, apparently written with AI's help, that puts a simple office suite right in your browser, with no logins or cloud access required.

It's called Tiny Little Office, and it comes from veteran developer and 'technology thinker' Paul Ford. There are 10 different components here: word processor, outliner, presentation tool, spreadsheet, calculator, drawing tool, diagram maker, animator, calendar, and trip planner. You can just click around and start working.

There's one main principle the office suite is built around: the link is the document. Any changes you make to a file are saved as codes in the URL itself, and sharing that URL shares an exact copy of the file. Someone else can take that URL and make their own edits (though they'll stay local and won't sync back with yours).

When you share links, they can be protected by passwords, configured as read only, and set to expire after a certain time period (from an hour to a month). For your own use, multiple files can be saved locally in the browser, or you can choose to wipe everything each time you close down the page.
Six years in the making
Introducing Tiny Little Office tinylittleoffice.com?c=xdgpfud#/v...
— @tinylittleoffice.bsky.social (@tinylittleoffice.bsky.social.bsky.social) 2026-10-16T13:08:46.635Z

The story of the project starts six years ago, when Ford's colleague Rich Ziade built TinySheet, a small ten-line spreadsheet that ran in the browser like Tiny Little Office does now. That was followed by TinyCalendar, but the projects were eventually abandoned, as were the URLs associated with them.

Now the idea is back as a full 10-app suite of products, because "it really is easier to build small than ever before". Ford says he uses the tool to leave himself notes in Slack, and that "if Signal was an operating system, this could, one day, aspire to be its productivity suite" due to its private, simple approach.

"There are lots of tradeoffs," adds Ford. "This is not, in any way, how web apps are expected to work. The links can get unwieldy pasted in chat, and you can't upload video or images, full stop. It's not collaborative like Google Docs. It's collaborative like handing out zines at a street fair."

articles.headline: Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola exchange heated jabs in Alaska Senate debate: Top takeaways
keyFacts: Sen. Dan Sullivan and former Rep. Mary Peltola exchanged heated jabs in their final televised Senate debate ahead of the upcoming general election.
The candidates clashed over Iran, energy prices, character accusations, and their respective distances from President Donald Trump.
The general election is scheduled to take place in two weeks.
body: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) and former Rep. Mary Peltola , a Democrat, exchanged jabs in the final televised debate between the top two Senate candidates in the 2026 cycle, with two weeks until the general election.

The debate touched on topics from Iran and affordability to President Donald Trump and attacks on character. While neither landed a decisive blow, the heated duel helped to cement the stakes in each party’s eyes ahead of the midterm elections .
Here are the biggest takeaways from Thursday’s debate:
Focus on Iran and energy

Iran and energy prices were a key focus of the debate, with Peltola attempting to pin both the war and higher prices on her GOP rival. Sullivan attempted to distance himself from Trump, offering measured criticism of the war. When asked about Trump’s decision to go to war unilaterally, Sullivan said, “Congress definitely should have been consulted.”
However, Sullivan still supported Trump’s war powers on Iran , as “the largest state sponsor of terrorism should not have nuclear weapons.” Despite this, he said that the war must end “soon.”
He also conceded that the energy costs “from this war are too high,” but that the way to bring them back down was “to produce more energy by and for Alaskans.”
Peltola, on the other hand, voiced support for ending the war without a peace deal, citing threats to the military.

“There does not appear to be a peace deal on the horizon, and I think it’s so important that our military be removed and protected,” she said when asked if she supported ending the war without a peace deal.
The war became central to her election pitch in the debate, saying it was “driving up our energy bills and hurting Alaskans with no end in sight.”
Sullivan hones in on Peltola’s character

The two candidates confronted accusations about their opponent’s personal character on the debate stage. Sullivan leaned into multiple reports that Peltola abused her staffers, using derogatory language behind the scenes.

“Twenty-five staffers quit on Mary Peltola because she abused them physically and emotionally, and then she slanders every other group, African Americans, special needs individuals,” Sullivan said. “It is a character flaw on my opponent.”
In one of her first public acknowledgments of the accusations, Peltola chalked it up to a few off days and “gossip.”
“I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth,” she said.
Pelotla took her own swipes at Sullivan’s character, accusing him of corruption and dishonesty.
“I think that Alaskans have had it up to here with the lying and dishonesty,” she said in one of her most viral moments. “Dan, you should be ashamed of yourself.”
Each candidate also sought to pin the other to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein , to which each countered with vigorous denials.
The specter of Trump

During the debate, Sullivan tried to separate himself from Trump on several policies while avoiding direct criticism of the president. He distanced himself from Trump on Ukraine, healthcare, and some of Trump’s past rhetoric. After he called out Peltola’s reported offensive remarks, she countered that he hadn’t pushed back on Trump’s past comments insulting women. Sullivan countered, saying he had pushed back on Trump’s previous insults against women.
Policywise, Sullivan hit Trump on his handling of Ukraine, saying the diesel deal with Russia was “not a good idea.”
“I just led the effort on a Russia sanctions act that passed Congress, so I’m opposed to that,” Sullivan said.
“Sometimes I oppose the Trump administration,” he said at one point.
The incumbent senator agreed with Peltola, saying a possible third term for Trump would be unconstitutional.
TRUMP AND LUTNICK SAY TAIWAN WILL PURCHASE 30% OF NATURAL GAS PRODUCED BY ALASKA PIPELINE PROJECT
A testy moment with notecards
At several points in the debate, Peltola appeared to be reading from notecards, drawing a quick accusation from Sullivan of an inside job.
“We weren’t supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?” he asked, prompting a vehement denial from the moderators.
“OK. I’m just watching my opponent,” Sullivan replied.
Peltola countered that she was better “prepared” than her opponent.
While Sullivan dropped the accusation of an inside job, he leaned into her heavy use of cards, posting about it numerous times on X, saying she needed “cue cards” and was reading off a script.
“Really, Mary? Reading off a script?” he said in one post . “You can’t cue-card your way through the Senate.”

keyFacts: With other hosts still on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump’s record-low poll numbers and beleaguered new press secretary, Katie Zacharia.

body: With other hosts still on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump’s record-low poll numbers and beleaguered new press secretary, Katie Zacharia.
Jimmy Kimmel
“We are only 19 days away from our president claiming that the elections were rigged,” said Kimmel on Thursday evening. “Never mind the fact that he is the one trying to rig them, of course.”
“Republicans got some very bad tidings from the fake liberal media,” as even the president’s former favorite, Fox News, predicts that Democrats will flip the House in the midterms.

The network “also betrayed daddy” with a new poll that said his approval rating is now at 36%, its lowest point ever, while traffic to Trump’s social media site, Truth Social, is down 30% year to year. “He seems to be the only one who posts to Truth Social,” said Kimmel. “And I seem to be the only one who reads those posts on Truth Social. It’s really just the two of us.”
“Don Jr hasn’t posted on Truth Social in two months,” he added. “Even Eric hasn’t posted since July. His own stupid sons have forsaken him!”

“But people are still showing up by the dozens to see him in person,” the host continued. “Trump has been touring and boring the country all this month, to remind voters what an amazing job he thinks he’s doing, and to castigate the fake news for not turning the cameras around to show the size of his crowds.”
At one of his rallies on Thursdays, Trump pursued such a point in his usual nonlinear fashion and wondered: “Is the camera like, statutory? Is it like a statue, you cannot move it?”
“Statutory – it’s a word he learned from his best friend Jeffrey Epstein,” Kimmel joked.

In other Trump news, the president announced that he would be cancelling Pete Hegseth’s plans to livestream a military execution by firing squad, because there are “many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die”.

The execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major and psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood in 2009, was set for 3 December. But Trump “had second thoughts after realizing that the man they would be executing is in a wheelchair”, Kimmel explained. “I guess he realized he’d have a hard time selling ads on a live stream of a paralyzed man being executed by firing squad, and what’s the point if he can’t make a little bit of money on it, right?”

“I wonder if he’ll show the same kind of mercy to his new future former press secretary,” Kimmel quipped, referring to Zacharia, Trump’s new press secretary whose first week on the job was less than stellar.

On Thursday, the former fringe network commentator tried to set the record state on questions about her statue as an attorney, and “it turns out that Katie Zacharia is an attorney in the same way George Santos was a volleyball champion,” Kimmel quipped. Zacharia has yet to confirm when or where she passed the bar exam; the Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia failed the California bar exam after graduating from law school there in 2011.

“His press secretary is supposed to be answering questions about his lies, not hers!” Kimmel added. “But the truth is, he didn’t hire her to be his lawyer. He didn’t really hire her to be his press secretary. He hired her so he could squeeze into a helicopter with her and Natalie” – Harp, his fellow blond assistant – “and rub his cankles against a woman’s legs without getting cursed out in Slovenian.”

body: “I hope so,” says Alonso. “Our goal is to keep doing that [scoring at this rate]. If we improve the level of scoring, and decrease numbers of conceding, we will be in a better way ... tomorrow at Everton will be tough ... I haven’t been to this stadium but they tell me it’s a nice one, with good atmosphere. I am looking forward to it.
“I want that we compete. We know it’s tough to win games away ... but we are able to deal with that ... for sure, the experience against Brentford is not forgotten.”
Potentially unpopular personal opinion alert: Perhaps Chelsea are outscoring their xG because xG is meaningless nonsense?
Will Chelsea’s activity in the January transfer window be affected by James’s injury?
“No. I don’t think so,” says Alonso. “We expect for that time he is back ... the timeline is not exact. But it will not affect it [activity in the January window.]
“He’s the captain. A very important player. He has a good mentality. We need him.”
James absence 'not going to be short', says Chelsea's Alonso

“We are disappointed, especially for him,” the Chelsea manager says of Reece James’s surgery on a knee injury. “In the last training he picked up an injury ... but now the surgery has been successful ... he will be close to the team, he is a great influence. We wish him the best recovery. We don’t set timelines, but he will be out for several weeks.

“It’s not going to be short. It’s not going to be two-three weeks ... time will tell. Things have to be done properly ... it’s a disappointment for everyone, for him ... we have a squad for that, to deal with the injuries.
“We have until the next break, four more Premier League games, a Cup game ... we will be able to manage well with the players we have ... we feel good.”
Has Maresca sought guidance on the current situation from anyone outside Manchester City?

“I am quite a ‘respect’ person,” Maresca says. “Everyone can say what they want ... I don’t have a problem with people having an opinion ... [but] I think it’s better to wait for the final words [the result of City’s appeal].

“I trust the club. I don’t need people from outside the club to understand the situation ... they explained the situation. It’s very clear. I trust them [City’s owners], this is the reason I joined the club.
“There is a lot of outside noise. We need to try and make our own noise. The different kind of noise, we are not able to control that.”
Pep Guardiola was at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday for the Champions League defeat by Paris Saint-Germain. Did Maresca speak to him?

“I saw him after the game. We were talking about the game, about the first half, about the second half ... he was very happy to be at the stadium, very positive about things he has seen during the game ... it was great for the fans to see him at the stadium ... this will always be his house.
Maresca feels 'no stress' about off-field issues at City

“Very happy. very pleased. Two big games, Liverpool away and PSG at home [in the past week]. We handled quite good, I think all together - the club, fans, teams, everyone. Tomorrow it’s the same points [on offer against Ipswich] as Anfield. That’s why it’s important we try to win.
“I am very happy. I don’t feel any kind of stress about the outside situation [verdict on financial charges]. It’s something I don’t control. I focus on how we can try to win the next games.

On Phil Foden: “He will score tomorrow. I just try to work with him, day by day. Since the international break, since the red card, he’s training well. Very positive, very good. He is available for tomorrow. No doubt he is going to give us something.”

Manchester City’s Enzo Maresca also had a chat with the media. He says it’s a “good moment” and a time to rotate players … and also that he is not focused on any records as a manager, after City’s perfect start. He is focused on Ipswich.
The Guardian’s Jamie Jackson asked Carrick if Martinez should have apologised personally to Jason Wilcox for his comments on Tuesday.
Carrick said: “He’s released his statement. That’s enough for us to move on with.
“From our point of view, the acknowledgement of what’s been done has been enough. We’ve moved on. We’re not looking it back now.

“I think I understand emotion at times. We ask for passion, emotion, fire, for players to care. There is a way of doing that and that’s been acknowledged. We need to carry that intensity and willingmess and use it in the right way.”
Carrick is asked – how can people outside believe that everything is OK, given the strength of Martinez’s comments?

“The players believe me. People talk from the outside. I am telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen for a while … Someone said something maybe they shouldn’t have, at a certain time … that doesn’t distract us from what we are creating here. I’m telling you, we are not affected. I thought there was a good reaction today.

“I don’t need results. We all do. It’s not about me. Manchester United is bigger than me … it’s not about me … I don’t go into work, or this game, thinking about me. It’s about the football club. What we stand for. What we live for. The history of what we need to live up to. It’s not about me.”
Carrick: Manchester United players have moved on after outburst, confirms Martinez is in squad
“It’s done. We’ve moved on. One of those things. He [Martinez] has come out and acknowledged the situation,” says Carrick.
“As a group we’ve moved on. Really not a drama for us. This morning [in training] there was a really good feeling around the squad. We’ve moved on really quickly.”
What was discussed internally?
“From the outside, you’re asking for big information, big discussions …

“It was pretty simple. We understood the situation and what it meant. He [Martinez] acknowledged it’s a mistake from him. And that was it, really. We’ve got a really good feeling in the group, within the club.
“Results-wise it’s not gone to plan but the spirit, the togetherness … today was one of the better training sessions we’ve had … we want to do something about this situation [on the pitch].
“We understand the situation, but it’s been dealt with, and we’ve moved on, genuinely moved on … there was a freshness about the group today that I really liked.”
Carrick confirms that Martinez is part of the squad for Sunday’s match at Leeds.
Spain have been fined $20,000 and ordered to partially close their stadium for the next friendly after fans chanted Islamophobic slogans during a game against Egypt in March, Fifa said.
The sanctions relate to incidents at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona, home of Espanyol, where some Spain fans chanted, “Who doesn’t jump is a Muslim” during a World Cup warmup match.
After the second occurrence of the chant, the stadium announcer issued a warning and the scoreboard displayed a message against discriminatory behaviour.
The Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants at the time, describing them as disrespectful and intolerable and calling those responsible “ignorant and racist“.
Spanish police launched an investigation the next day while world governing body Fifa later started disciplinary proceedings against the Spanish soccer federation (RFEF).

The RFEF argued that the word “Muslim” was “neither insulting nor pejorative“, adding the fans’ conduct should be assessed under Fifa’s Article 17, which covers political, ideological, religious or offensive messages, rather than Article 15, which deals with discrimination and racist abuse.

However, Fifa’s’s disciplinary committee rejected that argument, saying Article 15 does not require the explicit use of a slur and that a term can be discriminatory when used in context as “an insult, taunt, or marker of inferiority“.
Fifa fined the RFEF and ordered the closure of at least 15% of available seats for Spain’s next friendly. Reuters

Dionisi says report of Watford sacking 'fake news'

Despite reports suggesting he would be sacked if Watford lost at Cardiff on Tuesday, Alessio Dionisi remains in post. “There is good news, bad news or fake news probably,” the Italian told the BBC yesterday. “In this case for the moment, it is fake news. But I don’t decide.”

The situation at the club is dire: a squad haphazardly thrown together, with no money spent on transfer fees in the summer, the division’s lowest wage bill, few players arriving until the final days of the window, a miserable dearth of Championship experience (which the club leadership acknowledged and pledged to address at the end of last season, and for that matter before most recent transfer windows), a disjointed and lopsided squad notably bereft of midfield options, and an aloof and increasingly unpopular owner.

Since the start of March the club have played 21 league games and won only three, the worst record of any club which has been in the division throughout that time (indeed Coventry, Ipswich, West Ham and Oxford United all have more wins and more Championship points despite spending much of it in other divisions). Most recently they played Burnley at home when their opponents were bottom of the league and lost 4-0, and then went to 21st-placed Cardiff and lost 5-1. They are now 22nd, and both Elton John – who said he was “upset and disappointed at the decline” – and Troy Deeney have criticised the way they are playing and the way they are being run.

Tomorrow they host 13th-placed but also troubled Charlton, who won three of their first four league games but have not secured a victory since August.

Word is that the club has already made contact with potential replacements for Dionisi, but that the level of vitriol coming from those fans still sufficiently motivated to turn up to games has stayed Pozzo’s hand, for now. The club certainly have some players, the likes of Othmane Maamma and Myron Boadu, who are able to play at a much higher level to the one the team is currently showing, but do they have the motivation (and the teammates) to demonstrate that ability, or has the cycle of sackings drained the squad of all motivation and cohesion?
Coventry boss Frank Lampard is not prepared to relax after watching his side record back-to-back wins in the Premier League, writes the Press Association.

The Sky Blues looked to be in for a long season after losing their opening four games without scoring a goal. But they have kick-started their campaign with wins against Nottingham Forest and Newcastle and as he prepares to visit Tottenham on Monday Lampard wants to keep the foot on the gas.

“Keep driving it,” he said. “It’s very important to look at the the good things out of the game, also the things we can improve. But when we talk about the good things, I’m not overly patting them on the back because we have to work hard to get better.

“Every game brings different challenges, so I think the players understand me and my approach and the staff’s approach here. We never want to rest. I don’t. I’m always fearful of resting on something and thinking that you’ve made it. This league’s too difficult for that.
“So one of my first jobs is to keep pushing from that front, and the players need to feel that.”

Fulham fans fretting about life under Álvaro Arbeloa will not feel any better when they remember how things were under Marco Silva, who was one of the most effective managers in the Premier League when it came to making substitutions.

Silva’s substitutes were involved in the fourth-highest goal contributions last season and the most in the 2024-25 season. Fulham knew how to dig in and salvage unlikely points. But Silva left last summer, joining Benfica after concluding he could achieve nothing more at Craven Cottage, and his replacement is already under pressure after some puzzling tactical choices.

The worrying shift under Arbeloa was evident during Fulham’s collapse against Ipswich last weekend. The west Londoners were 1-0 up and looking good for their first league win of the season when Arbeloa weakened his midfield by replacing Shea Charles with Manuel Ángel in the 70th minute.

It was a strange way to shut up shop. Charles is physically imposing, has impressed since joining from Southampton and was doing well alongside Sander Berge. The 22-year-old Ángel is 5ft 7in, was making his Premier League debut and has little experience of senior football. Ipswich’s comeback to win 2-1 was not a surprise, particularly when Arbeloa’s other rejigs included bringing on Rodrigo Muniz and switching from a 4-2-3-1 system to a flat 4-4-2 in an attempt to defend the lead.

articles.headline: GTA 6 Is Taking Over Miami Amid Pushback From Officials: “We’re Depicting Miami Like A Murder Capital”
keyFacts: Rockstar is conducting major real-life marketing campaigns in Miami ahead of the November release of GTA 6.
Multiple Miami-Dade County commissioners criticized the partnership, stating the game portrays Miami as a murder capital.
Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava defended the partnership, hoping to generate millions in revenue.
body: GTA 6's takeover of real-life Miami is continuing, and in a big way, ahead of the open-world crime game's release in November. For anyone unaware, GTA 6 takes place in Vice City, which is a stand-in for Miami, and the game also takes players to surrounding areas of its version of Florida, known as Leonida.

After the GTA 6 logo was airlifted onto Miami's Kaseya Earlier this month to promote the game and an upcoming Miami Heat x GTA 6 crossover , Rockstar's marketing efforts have now grown substantially. This has included a number of real-life marketing activations in the Miami area covering real cars, blimps, beach chairs, and more.

The efforts have not been without controversy. Multiple Miami-Dade County commissioners expressed serious concerns about the city taking Rockstar's money to promote a game about violence and murder, among other ... vices.

"We're depicting Miami like a murder capital," Commissioner René Garcia said, according to the Miami Herald. Commissioner Micky Steinberg added: "Philosophically, I feel we should not be moving forward."

Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava and her office is hoping to bring in millions from its partnership with Rockstar to promote GTA 6 in Miami. Her chief of staff, Chris Hudtwalcker, said the GTA 6 takeovers in Miami are a "love letter" to the city.
Another lawmaker, chairman Anthony Rodriguez, said commissioners should remember GTA 6 is a work of fiction. "We are all adults in this community. We recognize it's just a game," he said.

"We cut our nose to spite our face," said Chair Anthony Rodriguez, who sponsored the legislation authorizing the negotiations. He urged commissioners not to go overboard on concern for made-up plot lines and digital characters. "This is a fictional game. We are all adults in this community. … We recognize it's just a game."

People in Miami have reported seeing GTA-style cars on the city streets, along with a massive Vice City blimp soaring overhead. What's more, branded beach chairs and umbrellas are being dispatched to beaches in south Florida to market GTA 6. The marketing efforts for GTA 6 go beyond Miami, of course, as people have begun to spot big ads in other major American cities like Chicago and New York.

articles.headline: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
keyFacts: Joshua Foster was fined 3,000 euros by a Cyprus court for causing the death of his two-year-old son.
The toddler fell nearly 40 feet from a fourth-floor hotel window after Foster placed him on the sill to view a waterpark.
The judge stated there was no evidence Foster deliberately exposed the child to danger, calling it a momentary error.
body: - Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His failure to establish that the window was closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences."
The judge said there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

articles.headline: Warhammer: Boltgun 2 Is Basically A Perfect Sequel To One Of 2023’s Best Shooters
keyFacts: Kotaku reported that the video game Warhammer: Boltgun 2 is now available as a sequel to the 2023 shooter.
Kotaku stated that players can choose between two characters, Malum Caedo and Nyla Veyrath, who feature different combat styles and weapons.
Kotaku noted that the sequel offers increased variety with new environments, enemies, and improved level design.
body: A few years back, Warhammer: Boltgun hit PC and console and won me over with its snappy combat, crunchy retro visuals, and dark humor that made it clear that the people who built the game understood the universe of W40k. And at first, Boltgun 2, out now, didn’t seem like a huge improvement over the last game. But as I’ve played more, I’ve discovered that this new sequel is bigger and better in every way.

Boltgun 2 is set directly after the events of the first game, but you don’t need to have played that game to hop into this one. Long story short, you play as a tough-as-nails Space Marine who is focused on one thing: Destroying enemies of the Imperium of Man and doing it as brutally and effectively as possible. This involves a lot of shooting and explosions. Heretics tend to put up a fight.

This time around, however, players can take up the fight against heretical demons and soldiers as either returning protagonist Malum Caedo or new playable character and badass Battle Sister Nyla Veyrath. Both are very deadly warriors, but they get the job done differently. Malum hits hard and moves slower. He also uses guns from the first game, like the titular boltgun and the immensely satisfying-to-fire shotgun. Meanwhile, Nyla is more nimble and has a different array of firearms that include a flamethrower and a powerful crossbow.

As you complete levels in the main campaign as one character, you can go back and replay them as the other whenever you want. While they don’t shake things up so dramatically that I felt the need to replay every level twice, I did enjoy how different they felt moment-to-moment, offering me the chance to be faster or heavier depending on the combat encounters in each level.

The other big improvement in Boltgun 2 is the increase in overall variety. In the first game, it could start to feel like you were exploring similar halls and shooting the same enemies over and over. In Boltgun 2, there’s a much wider variety of both environments to see and enemies to kill. At first, I was fighting armed cultists in a big, gothic space castle. Then I was killing zombies and toads in a creepy swamp biome. Later, I was dodging snipers and red demons in a nightmarish hellscape.
All these different places to explore make Boltgun 2 feel bigger and more like an epic Warhammer 40k adventure. And I appreciate the improved level design in the sequel.

The first game far too frequently made players fight large waves of enemies in closed-off arenas. It was fun, but could get tedious. Boltgun 2 features levels that feel ripped out of the ’90s and early ’00s shooters it’s clearly inspired by, with winding pathways and big rooms that connect to smaller areas that loop around. It makes combat encounters more varied and overall makes Boltgun 2 feel more sprawling, but in a good way. And if you ever get lost or turned around, you can tap a button to spawn a line on the ground that points you to your main objective.

The main campaign so far has been a blast, featuring different levels that you have to choose between as you progress through the game’s story. I’m really digging all of the new weapons, the improved level design, and the bigger roster of monsters and enemies to blast away. Boltgun 2 really does feel like the perfect sequel to an already stellar game, and if by the end of its runtime I’m still enjoying its maps and action, it will likely be on my list of best shooters of 2026.

articles.headline: The ‘frenemy’ reality: Why America is miscalculating its greatest economic challenge
keyFacts: Washington mischaracterizes China as an ideological communist enemy, causing the United States to miscalculate its strategic response to a state-directed capitalist rival, according to the article.
Data analyzed by the Harvard Kennedy School shows China’s private sector generates about 60 percent of its gross domestic product and drives over 80 percent of urban employment.
The authors state that America must shift its focus from bloated defense contracts to competitive domestic investments, raw manufacturing capacity, and vital infrastructure to outperform China.
body: Following the recent meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping , the media have generally focused on immediate transactional outcomes such as the extension of the trade truce, high-tech competition in artificial intelligence, and the geopolitical flashpoint of Taiwan.

For many years, Washington’s foreign policy status quo has mischaracterized the Chinese Communist Party as an ideological monolith hell-bent on spreading global Marxism. This misdiagnosis causes the United States to miscalculate its strategic response. Navigating this 21st-century undertaking requires confronting what China actually is: a centralized, nationalist dictatorship running a deeply integrated, state-directed market economy. China seeks to dominate the world economically.

Washington clings to the “ communist ” label because an ideological enemy provides domestic leverage over strategic clarity. The political Right focuses on invasion threats to expand conventional defense budgets. Meanwhile, the political Left frames the struggle as a moral crusade to highlight human rights violations and surveillance. Both factions employ this framing because outside threats allow a divided Congress to bypass gridlock and pass bloated spending bills. This distortion begins in the classroom. Standard U.S. textbooks still default to the “communist” moniker, leaving young people with the false impression that they face a stagnant, Soviet-style command economy rather than a state-directed capitalistic rival.

The reality is that China poses an economic and technological challenge, not an ideological one. True communism requires the absolute abolition of private property and total state ownership of production. Modern China does not operate this way. Following late 20th-century market reforms, Beijing embraced an authoritarian capitalist model. Today, China boasts an active stock exchange and hosts over 1,110 billionaires on the Hurun Global Rich List. Data analyzed by the Harvard Kennedy School reveals that China’s domestic private sector generates approximately 60% of its gross domestic product and drives over 80% of urban employment. Marxist purists would view contemporary Beijing not as a triumph of their ideology, but as its ultimate distortion.

This state-directed capitalist landscape is further illustrated by the market-driven activities operating within and across China’s borders. The global surge in fentanyl precursor manufacturing, underground banking syndicates, and transnational human trafficking rings are consequences of unregulated market forces, not communist doctrine. In a textbook command economy, these decentralized, profit-seeking operations would be structurally impossible. Independent Chinese chemical factories supply precursor elements to Mexican cartels with an entrepreneurial agility that mimics Western corporate supply chains, driven purely by financial gain.

Simultaneously, state-subsidized corporations flood global markets with cheap consumer devices, heavy industrial equipment, and green technology. Even when the environmental impacts are recognized, they are ignored in pursuit of global market share. Western consumers, drawn by unmatched price points, buy these goods, effectively subsidizing China’s externalized environmental costs. This behavior demonstrates the cold calculus of market extraction and value-shifting to capture market dominance, rather than a planned economy focused on collective welfare. Yet, Washington defaults to its old playbook, treating a competitive corporate extraction model as a mid-century ideological campaign.

None of this excuses totalitarian abuses within China’s borders. As documented in country reports by the Department of State, Beijing enforces a digital surveillance state, systematically oppresses minorities in Xinjiang, and stifles free political speech. Yet, Washington’s outrage remains highly selective, routinely overlooking identical behavior from strategic allies, ranging from Middle Eastern oil regimes to Western-aligned security partners. This double standard betrays the truth: the “communist” label is a convenient rhetorical weapon to justify economic protectionism and defense spending rather than a true reflection of moral consistency.

Beijing has no interest in converting the people to Marxism or exporting a cultural revolution. Its objectives are winning the trade war, controlling global production, dominating supply chains, and displacing American economic hegemony. By treating China merely as an economic rival, Washington would have to engage in rigorous domestic industrial policy and economic discipline. Instead, politicians default to rhetorical grandstanding while moving away from market liberalization toward protective bilateral trade marked by export bans and tech regulations.

This foreign policy hides a darker reality: Washington is actively instigating the world order it claims to protect against. Isolating near-peer economic opponents through sweeping financial blockades has forced a volatile geopolitical alignment, driving China and Russia into strategic partnerships with hostile regimes such as Iran and North Korea. Left to their own devices, these major market superpowers would prefer stable, predictable, and cooperative trading relationships with the West rather than a consolidated axis of convenience.

Treating China just like the old Soviet Union causes Washington to fundamentally miscalculate its leverage. China is deeply woven into global supply chains. A Peterson Institute for International Economics analysis highlights that despite heightened tariffs, value-added trade data reveals a deep underlying economic interdependence that simple import metrics mask. Chinese components are merely rerouted through third-party countries such as Vietnam or Mexico before reaching American consumers. We cannot decouple from a global market giant using a playbook designed for an isolated, virtually closed nation.

Furthermore, viewing the relationship through an ideological lens causes Washington to hyperfixate on regional flashpoints like Taiwan while missing the wider structural competition. The root challenge is that an autocratic superpower seeks to displace American economic, financial, and technological leadership. Rather than addressing the core economic structures that make China competitive, lawmakers target American tech companies in defense authorization bills while keeping traditional defense spending high.
WASHINGTON’S AI MORATORIUM IS THE BEST GIFT XI JINPING COULD ASK FOR

When politicians focus entirely on communism, they search for the wrong warning signs. They should be looking at port infrastructure, rare-earth monopolies, and artificial intelligence laboratories. As documented by the Council on Foreign Relations, China is expanding its footprint via state-backed capitalism and its multitrillion-dollar Belt and Road Initiative. You cannot defeat a state-sponsored corporate juggernaut with anti-communist lectures.

The current trajectory is unsustainable. Shifting focus from bloated defense contracts toward competitive domestic investments in cutting-edge technology , raw manufacturing capacity, and vital infrastructure is the only viable path. True normalization will not come from demanding ideological surrender from Beijing, nor from manufacturing a permanent adversarial standoff to satisfy Washington’s military-industrial complex. It will come when America secures its own economic resilience, projects strength through financial independence, and negotiates from a position of undisputed domestic success. Only when we accurately outline China’s state-directed model can we construct a strategy pragmatic enough to outperform it.

Cheryl-Ann Lee-Llacer Wargotz is an economic researcher and a former network manager with a background in economics and private asset administration. Her interests focus on the intersection of global trade networks and the growth of the high-tech workforce. Eric Wargotz, M.D., is a geopolitical analyst and policy commentator who has held leadership roles across government and medicine. A clinical professor emeritus at George Washington University and judge, he is a former U.S. Senate nominee and elected county commission president. Views expressed are their own.

articles.headline: Technics EAH-A1000 review: Superior sound and excellent ANC in a premium package
keyFacts: Technics released the $450 EAH-A1000 over-ear wireless headphones featuring magnetic fluid drivers and adaptive active noise cancellation.
The reviewer stated that the headphones offer superior sound quality, tight bass, and effective noise cancellation.
The reviewer noted that the headphones compete well with rival models from Sony and Sennheiser despite some minor button control issues.
body: Technics EAH-A1000 review: Superior sound and excellent ANC in a premium package
The company's flagship over-ear wireless headphones are light on compromises, but enter a competitive market.

When Technics announced the EAH-A1000 over-ear Bluetooth headphones, everything seemed fairly ordinary. Another set of premium cans entering an already crowded category. Sure, they have a few standout features on the spec sheet — magnetic fluid drivers and three-device multipoint Bluetooth, for example. At $450, they are directly taking on Sony's popular WH-1000XM6, and almost enter the same territory as Sennheiser's audiophile-friendly HDB 630.

It's a confident move from Technics, to place its flag in the lucrative, but risky, territory between high-end consumer and "affordable" specialist headphones. I've had the A1000 on the testing bench (a.k.a. my head) for a couple of weeks and my initial assessment of how "ordinary" they are might have been a little hasty.
What's new on the Technics EAH-A1000?

The feature Technics is making the most noise about is the "Magnetic Fluid" technology, but it's not new to the A1000. The AZ100 true wireless earbuds also use it, but these are the first over-ears from Technics to include it. The idea is that it reduces unwanted vibrations in the driver, in turn reducing distortion.

One other feature that stands out is the three-device multipoint Bluetooth. Seamless connection with your phone and PC can now include one more device, like a gaming console or TV. There is a slight limitation here: If you listen via LDAC (which the A1000 also supports), that will limit you to two devices maximum.

Of course there's adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC) coupled with a beamforming microphone for clearer phone calls. Other features you'd expect at this price point, such as Dolby Atmos with headtracking, wear detection, EQ/app control, a healthy 45-hour battery life (with ANC on) and lossless playback via USB-C and 3.5mm cables (both provided) are all present and correct. Cosmetically, the A1000 offers smooth lines and a stylish, but understated, design. They could pass for a Sony or Bose model at a glance.
Audio and ANC performance

Headphone marketing materials are like gourmet menus: There are a lot of decorative adjectives to describe beef. Or, in the case of headphones, 40mm drivers. I can't put my hand on my heart and say that the magnetic fluid technology Technics mentions is making a difference, but I was immediately impressed when I first put the A1000 on and pressed play on Spotify.

My music tastes skew electronic, so bass really matters. On the A1000, the low frequencies are some of the tightest I've heard. That's the best word I can find for it. The bass is present, I can feel it, but it's not vibrating in my eardrums at all. It sounds like it's firmly attached to the song with glue, in a good way. Kick drums in dance music offer a gentle thwack, in turn providing a good sense of space and dynamic range in the mix.

Pop and rock genres do a good job at exposing the mid and high frequencies. BTS' Dynamite, for example, sounds much more robust and balanced in the A1000 than it does in my car on the school run when I'm trying to animate the kids. I even heard parts of the bassline I barely knew existed. If there's a minor criticism, it's at the higher end. Listening to AC/DC or the Arctic Monkeys, the guitars sound authentic, but my ears wanted a teeny-tiny bit more sizzle out of them.

I regularly use the Sennheiser HDB 630 and the Technics A1000 surprised me with a slightly bigger sense of space and soundstage. The tight balance and well-rounded bass make them one of the strongest pairs I've tried for a long time.

The stellar sound wasn't the first thing I noticed when I put them on, the adaptive ANC is also extremely good. I'm a little fussy with noise cancellation; it's a feature I appreciate but I prefer good audio chops over superior ANC if I have to choose. With the A1000, that's not really an issue. The noise cancellation is effective for both steady sounds like fans, yet it's adaptive enough that I can't hear people talking when my spouse has guests and I'm working. I prefer it to the ANC on the HDB 630 and I'd say it's good enough to be in the same room with Sony and Bose.
App and controls

I have a folder on my phone that's a graveyard of unused headphone apps. Technics Connect hasn't made it there, yet. As control apps go, it's easy to navigate and you'll find extra settings like choosing between LDAC compatible multipoint Bluetooth (remember: max two connections) or even turning it off. There's the aforementioned EQ section, the option to choose how long before the headphones auto-turn off and a toggle to disable wear detection, among other fine helpful tools.

A note on the multipoint feature: I've never really had a good experience with it on any headphones, with my Mac usually connecting via the hands-free profile. That was my experience with the A1000, too. Even switching between my phone and my Windows laptop was unreliable. I can't confidently blame these headphones, but I didn't have much luck with two devices, let alone three.

There are no touch controls on the A1000, instead you get two buttons and a clickable volume rocker. Despite everything being on the right earcup, it doesn't feel cramped. The volume rocker is easy to find, but you click "back" for volume up, which feels counter intuitive to me. Media controls are navigated by multiple clicks on the same rocker. It's practical and works, but sometimes the button lightly sticks, turning three clicks into two, which is the difference between a skip forward and skip back.
The competition

The $449 pits the A1000 directly against Sony's WH-1000XM6, and I do think it competes well on sound quality and ANC. The choice will come down to secondary details like design and battery life and app features, with the latter being where Sony really stacks the deck. I'll come right out and say that I personally prefer the A1000 to the $500 Sennheiser HDB 630. Technics might not quite beat them on sound, but it's really close. For ANC, comfort and build quality, for me Technics takes the win. Sonos' Ace Ultra matches the A1000 for price, and Engadget rated them highly, in part for their compatibility with Sonos speakers.
Wrap-up

For a legacy hi-fi brand, Technics has taken the long road when it comes to consumer headphones. The true wireless AZ100 made a big impression, thanks in part to those Magnetic Fluid drivers, and the A1000 builds on that success with equally impressive sound. Truly, they're a joy to wear and to listen to. There are also enough extra details, like a beam-forming microphone that destroys background noise with what feels like witchcraft (even if the mic itself is just so-so).

The sticking point for some will be the price. Sennheiser can ask more for the HDB 630 thanks to its long, unbroken record with good consumer headphones. You also get the $60 BTD 700 dongle thrown in. Meanwhile, Sony has built a steady reputation with its 1000X line over the last few years. Technics doesn't have the same recent pedigree, yet, but the A1000 does a really good job at kicking that off.
