articles.headline: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
keyFacts: Replit CEO Amjad Masad stated at TechCrunch Disrupt that AI agents will create a self-driving company model where they handle grunt work.
Masad explained that at Replit, AI agents triage support tickets and deploy fixes, requiring humans to provide essential judgment and taste.
Masad said that instead of replacing human jobs, AI agents shift workers to focus more on architecture, planning, and creative tasks.
body: Replit CEO and co-founder, Amjad Masad, has seen how AI is impacting the workplace first-hand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.

He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste.

“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.

“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”

Illustrating the shift, the Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.

“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.

“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”

He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said).
“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

articles.headline: Germany, France agree on deal to support Europe's struggling car industry
keyFacts: Germany and France agreed on a plan to support Europe's automotive industry and cut CO2 emissions.
Leaders including German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron welcomed the agreement.
The pact requires backing from other European Union states and the European Parliament to become law.
body: Germany and France have reached a deal to protect Europe's automotive industry, the countries said in a statement Friday.
The plan aims to cut CO2 emissions and support the development and construction of electric cars in Europe, the statement added.

"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the countries said.
The pact also includes incentives for investment, research and production.
Leaders welcome agreement
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz welcomed the agreement, describing it as a "good day for car drivers and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe."
"This is an investment signal to industry," he posted on his X account.
French President Emmanuel Macron, for his part, said the agreement shows a "clear ambition to successfully transform" the European automotive industry while upholding Europe's climate goals.
"We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry," Macron wrote.

According to a Handelsblatt report, the two leaders have also agreed in principle to require automakers to cut exhaust emissions from new cars by 90% from 2035, without having to offset the remaining 10%, revising the bloc's proposed target.
The pact will need backing from other EU states and the European Parliament to become law.
Europe's automotive industry faces tough competition from China
European car makers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies hailed the agreement as a "strong signal" in support of Europe's car industry that protects jobs in the sector.
Lower Saxony is where German automotive giant Volkswagen's headquarters are located, in the city of Wolfsburg. Lies is also part of VW's supervisory board.
Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.
As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.

articles.headline: iPhone Duo Preorders Sell Out in Minutes: Backordered Until January
keyFacts: Preorders for Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, sold out within minutes and are now backordered until January.
The iPhone Duo features a 7.6-inch main screen, two 48-megapixel cameras, Apple Pencil support, and a starting price of $1,999.
Customers hoping to get the phone sooner can attempt to purchase one in stores on its October 23 release date.
body: Apple’s iPhone Duo, its first foldable phone, is a hot ticket, judging by the preorders.

Preorders for the iPhone Duo began on Friday at 5 a.m. PT, on Apple’s website and the Apple Store app. Although the phone has an Oct. 23 release date, as of now preordered models won’t ship until Jan. 29. If you want the phone sooner than 2027, you can try to buy one in stores on Oct. 23.

CNET Senior Tech Reporter Abrar Al Heeti got to handle the iPhone Duo briefly ahead of preorders, and described it as essentially a compact iPhone that can double as an iPad Mini, well suited for consuming media. Beyond that, she wrote, “It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on.”

The 7.6-inch screen when opened is the largest iPhone display screen yet (there’s also a 5.4-inch outer display). The Duo is also equipped with two 48-megapixel cameras: a main camera and an ultrawide one. It’s geared for multitasking, with Apple Pencil support and drag-and-drop functionality similar to an iPad.
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999, but trade-in offers and Apple’s Upgrade program could lower how much you pay out of pocket.

Apple is years late to the folding phone market, though that might not matter much to those already in the iPhone ecosystem. The bigger question is whether the iPhone Duo will be tempting to those inclined to buy Android phones, where the latest hinged options include the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 and Galaxy Flip 8 and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold.

articles.headline: The Sony Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting a promised update to Android 17
keyFacts: Sony announced that the Xperia 10 VI will not receive the previously promised Android 17 update.
Sony stated that a technical assessment revealed storage limitations prevent an adequate upgrade experience on the device.
Sony will continue to provide four years of security updates for the phone until June 2028.
body: When the midrange Sony Xperia 10 VI was announced over two years ago with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 6 Gen 1 chipset and Android 14, Sony promised three major OS updates which would have included this year’s Android 17 release. However, according to a notice posted to the company’s UK support site, the Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting Android 17 after all.
The Sony Xperia 10 VI won’t be getting a promised update to Android 17
Three OS updates were promised when the phone launched but Sony says that won’t happen as a result of a storage issue.

In the notice Sony explains that a “detailed technical assessment” revealed that “limitations related to the device’s storage configuration” mean the Xperia 10 VI “does not support an Android 17 upgrade experience that we consider adequate.” As a result, the company has “decided not to make this upgrade available” and apologized that the decision “falls short of our original announcement.”

Sony clarifies that while OS updates for the Xperia 10 VI are ending, the company will continue to provide four years of security updates which should extend until June 2028. Sony also points out that this specific issue only applies to the “Xperia 10 VI’s technical specifications” and does not impact promised OS updates for other Xperia models. But since the technical requirements of future versions of Android aren’t yet known, it’s hard to take Sony at its word given today’s announcement.

articles.headline: NRL gap a factor in France's heavy defeat by Samoa, says boss
keyFacts: France head coach Laurent Frayssinous attributed his team's 78-4 defeat by Samoa to the growing performance gap between the NRL and Super League.
Samoa secured the emphatic victory with 14 tries, including four scored by substitute Sua Fa'alogo in Parramatta.
Frayssinous stated he would welcome proposed investment from the NRL into the European Super League.
body: - Published
France head coach Laurent Frayssinous suggested the growing gap between the NRL and Super League was a huge factor in Friday's 78-4 defeat by Samoa at the Men's Rugby League World Cup.
Melbourne storm winger Sua Fa'alogo came off the bench as a replacement for the injured Deine Mariner to score four of Samoa's 14 tries in an emphatic Pool B-C victory in Parramatta.

Mariner had opened the scoring, with two tries for Benaiah Ioelu and one each for Jermaine McEwen, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Stephen Crichton, Shawn Blore, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Izack Tago and Francis Molo. France's sole try came in the first half from Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet.

Frayssinous admitted his team were "all over the shop" in an opening 20 minutes where Samoa scored five times - with France not helped by head injuries to winger Leo Darrelatour and stand-off Cesar Rouge, although the latter was able to return after an assessment.

But, asked why France had fallen to an even heavier defeat than the 62-4 loss they suffered against Samoa in Warrington at the last World Cup four years ago, Frayssinous pointed to the level of NRL talent in the opposing ranks.
"I have a question for you," Frayssinous said. "Do you think the NRL is far better now than four years ago? Then you have the answer."

All but one of the Samoa squad are with clubs in the NRL, while France's team is largely made up of Super League players, although they do have South Sydney Rabbitohs centre Latrell Siegwalt in their line-up.
"The NRL keeps growing and keeps getting better every year," Frayssinous added. "Watching NRL every year, it's at the top, at the top, at the top. A step up, step up, step up.

"Does that mean Super League isn't? No. Super League is [getting] better every year, but not as fast as the NRL. The smartness, the skill the guys have under pressure, the touches, week in, week out, that's something we need to improve in Super League, simple as that."
Frayssinous made clear he would welcome the NRL's proposed investment in Super League.
"Definitely," he said. "What the NRL has done here is so good, what they bring to the game is great, so we want the NRL to do it the same in Europe."
Fa'alogo's performance as a replacement for Mariner - who will have a scan on a hamstring strain - demonstrated Samoa's strength in depth, as their head coach Ben Gardiner acknowledged.
"We were planning for him [Fa'alogo] to play at some stage, and he just got on a bit earlier than he probably would have thought," Gardiner said. "And to his credit, he went out and had a blinder."
Rugby League World Cup
15 October - 15 November
Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand
Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app
'Scrappy' Australia start with win - and seek to build support

Australia are widely expected to win a fourth successive Women's Rugby League World Cup, but a 40-0 victory over Samoa in their Pool A opener still had head coach Jess Skinner seeking improvement - in the stands as well as on the pitch.

Samoa, playing at the women's World Cup for the first time since 2008, were much better than the scoreline suggested, defending their try-line superbly and causing the co-hosts problems without being able to convert pressure into points.

Stand-off Jocelyn Kelleher was the standout Australia player on her debut - her kicking game was superb - and the defending champions scored seven tries without reply, through Jaime Chapman, Julia Robinson, Shaylee Bent, Keeley Nizza, Olivia Kernick, Keilee Joseph and Jessica Sergis.
Skinner, though, wants to see Australia cut out errors before they face England in Perth a week on Saturday.
"There are lots of work-ons for us moving forward," Skinner said. "It was a little bit scrappy at times.

"We need to work on our starts, and we need some high finishes to end our sets and probably some strong defence in the first three tackles. But overall, there were lots of little wins to be proud of."
Skinner also called on the crowds to be more supportive of the women's game at this World Cup.

Australia's opener at Western Sydney Stadium in Parramatta was staged as the second part of a double-header with the men's match between France and Samoa - with a number of fans not staying to watch the defending champions.

"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.
"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."

articles.headline: Ubisoft were working on a second Assassin's Creed game set in Qin Dynasty China, if this allegedly leaked footage is to be believed
keyFacts: Footage of a cancelled Assassin's Creed game titled Destiny has allegedly leaked online from developer portfolios.
MP1st reported the PC and console game was set in 206 BCE China and developed by Tencent's TiMi Studio Group.
The project was reportedly cancelled because Tencent decided to scale back from working on big-name Western series.
body: Footage alleged to show a prototype of a cancelled Assassin’s Creed game in action has popped up online. The game, it's claimed, was set in ancient China, went by the working title Assassin’s Creed Destiny, and was a separate project to Chinese-set mobile game Assassin’s Creed Jade. Instead, from the sounds of it Destiny would have been a game aimed at PC and consoles.

MP1st claim to have unearthed this in-development look at AC ThatBungieShooter from developer portfolios and that the game was being headed by Tencent Games subsidiary TiMi Studio Group. Set in the Qin Dynasty period - as the still in the works Jade is - AC Destiny's events would reportedly have taken place in 206 BCE, putting a few years of distance between the two.

The majority of the alleged Destiny footage shows a female assassin fighting her way into a sacred palace that's under siege by real world Chinese warlord Xiang Yu, with possession of a mysterious artefact on the line. Very much an Assassin's Creed game, then. Those hooded roof-jumpers do love their shiny baubles of indeterminate power. There's also some footage of fighting animations playing out in the grey-walled prisons of dev testing environments.

Destiny appears to have gotten the axe following Tencent's decision to scale back from working on big-name Western series in favour of upping their focus on a select pool of big budget games that don't come with chunky royalty fees to other firms.

Assassin's Creed Jade didn't end up getting the axe, but does still remain without a release date as of writing. It was last briefly mentioned by Ubisoft during a March rundown of everything going on Assassin's Creed land from the series' head of content Jean Guesdon.

If you're after an AC game set in China that you can play on PC, 2015's Assassin’s Creed Chronicles: China exists. It's a 2.5D spot of stabbing set during the Ming dynasty and stars Ezio-trained female assassin Shao Jun. It's also where I got the featured image for this article, though I must stress it's not one I've played - it lurks within the lengthy list of ACs I might eventually get to if I get time between now and the end of time.

articles.headline: Trump's Capitol Hill whisperer reveals secrets to president's dealmaking as he heads for exit
keyFacts: James Braid stepped down on Tuesday after serving as director of the Office of Legislative Affairs, where he helped advance President Donald Trump's agenda on Capitol Hill.
Braid stated that working on Trump's legislative priorities involved navigating tensions with lawmakers and maintaining optimism through difficult negotiations.
Katie Bailey, Braid's former deputy director, is taking over the position as Braid plans to take time off and figure out his next move.
body: EXCLUSIVE: There are few people in the United States who have more significantly shaped the course of American history over the last two years, while remaining as little-known as James Braid.

Millions of Americans across the country may not be familiar with the name, but in Washington, D.C., Braid is hard to miss both literally and figuratively. At 6 feet, 6 inches tall, he cast a tall shadow during his days at the White House and on Capitol Hill pushing President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda.

And that shadow has been responsible for helping push numerous legislative successes for Trump over the finish line, from rolling back Biden-era policies to passing Trump’s signature tax policy bill, until Tuesday — which marked Braid’s last day as director of the Office of Legislative Affairs. The "stock-in-trade" of the job, he told Fox News Digital in a rare interview, "is cautious optimism in the face of all odds."

From the outside, being Trump’s whisperer on Capitol Hill does not look like an easy job, particularly when the president is known to personally call out lawmakers who oppose his agenda. Recently, for example, he publicized the personal phone number of Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., over his opposition to a bill making daylight saving time permanent .
TRUMP DROPS REPUBLICAN SENATOR'S PHONE NUMBER IN SOCIAL POST OVER FURY ON STALLED BILL

But Braid insisted that Trump’s people skills ultimately meant those dust-ups came out of the wash and lauded "his extraordinary capacity to have a tough conversation one day and play a round of golf the next."

"There's always a give-and-take in any relationship with a legislator, and sometimes there's a give as a result of, you know, tension," Braid said. "But you know … one errant Truth [Social post], or one critical Truth, does not a relationship make."
But some Republicans’ relationships with the president never seemed to recover, like in the case of Sen. Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., who has no love lost with Trump.
Braid said the key to working with people was always being straightforward about what the White House wants.
"We've been able to be honest brokers and deliver for a lot of these members in different ways," he said.
But Trump’s presence still looms large in Congress whether he’s there in person or not.
A senior administration official familiar with Braid’s work told Fox News Digital that ultimately, "No one speaks for President Trump except for President Trump."
The official said Trump is known to be "hands-on at every critical legislative juncture" that pushes his agenda forward.
And Braid revealed that he keeps tabs on certain votes, as well.

"He always wants to know how people are voting after every major vote. He knows where people are," Braid said, adding that Trump "ultimately knows that Republicans in Congress overwhelmingly vote with him."
But Braid admitted he has faced long odds over his last two years, particularly with the vast tax-and-policy package nicknamed the Big, Beautiful Bill.
MILLIONS TAP TRUMP TAX CUTS THIS FILING SEASON AS REFUNDS TOP $3,400

He recalled sitting in his office one day, "I looked at the quad on the TV, and every single chyron is some variation of ‘GOP megabill in trouble.’ And yeah, I mean, there's certainly, at every moment, it was tenuous. At every moment, the thread was fraying."

One specific scenario he recalled took place at Sterling Golf Club in Virginia, where he, Trump, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought and then-deputy chief of staff James Blair were meeting with Senate Republican holdouts on the legislation.
GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

"We're sitting there with [Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky.], [Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.], [Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla.], me, Blair, Russ and the president, and they're bringing out these heaps of food," Braid recalled. "I think there's something like four pizzas on the table and maybe 22 hot dogs for five guys, none of them were eating. And it's just, I mean, we, I think we argued about the administration's overall funding strategy for two hours as the afternoon wore on."
Ultimately, however, the bill passed the House and Senate — for which Braid credited both administration officials and congressional leaders.
"The level of commitment that was there and present from the leadership across the Republican Party to get this thing done, basically willed it into being," he said.

He referenced the day Trump signed the bill when asked about his best day on the job over the last two years: "I would say July 4th in the White House with my son and the speaker of the House in the summer sunshine, watching the president sign the most significant piece of Republican domestic policy legislation."
Top congressional leaders hailed Braid as a critical champion of the GOP agenda.

"James is a total pro and one of House Republicans’ greatest teammates," House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., said. "He took the time to get to know our members and master the unique dynamics of the House Republican Conference."
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called Braid a "tremendous partner" for his conference.
"I’m grateful for his dedicated service to our country, and I wish him and his family all the best with their next chapter," Thune said.
Vought called Braid a "lion for the president in delivering his agenda on the Hill."

And Vice President JD Vance, who hired Braid as his legislative director before both ascended to the White House, told Fox News Digital that he is "incredibly brilliant, effective and a hard worker without compare."

"He has been with me since the start of my Senate term, where he was with me for every fight and brought his talents to the president’s second term, where he has played a central role in every single policy effort since," Vance said.

Now that he is departing, the senior administration official who spoke with Fox News Digital said they expect Braid to find work outside the government after years of grinding on Capitol Hill and the White House.

As for Braid, he said of his next move, "It's hard for me to even think about not doing this job, but at the end of the day, I know [Katie Bailey is] going to do great … but yeah, I'll take a little time and try to figure out what's next."
Bailey, Braid's former deputy director of the Office of Legislative Affairs, is now taking over the job.
He summed up his advice to his successor in two bullet points.

"Number one, you have to be ruthless in what you're focused on and tune out the distractions to get the issue of the day over the line and onto the president's desk," he said. "Number two, invariably, the situation feels pretty grave, but usually we muddle through, and to remain optimistic."

articles.headline: 'Crystal Lake' Ending Explained: Jason Voorhees' New Origin Story and More
keyFacts: Showrunner Brad Caleb Kane's new television series Crystal Lake alters the timeline and establishes a new origin story for Jason and Pamela Voorhees.
Episode 7 reveals that a young Pamela enrolled in a corporate experiment during the Cold War to save her failing pregnancy, leading to Jason's invulnerability.
The series suggests that Pamela's transformation into a serial killer was driven by grief combined with severe brain chemistry changes from quitting prescribed medication.
body: Brad Caleb Kane is ready to take on the haters. That's a good thing, because his new show, Crystal Lake, is almost guaranteed to be met with criticism from riled-up Friday the 13th fans angry over the changes Kane is making to Jason Voorhees canon in his attempt to give slasher icon Jason and his murderous mother Pamela (Linda Cardellini) a fleshed-out backstory.

For one thing, Crystal Lake reshuffles the original timeline, moving Jason's death up from 1957 to 1971, and then compresses the amount of time between that event and the summer camp slaughter that follows.
"I think the mythology is a little wonky as it is in terms of the timeline," Kane says, somewhat defensively, when I bring up these timeline shifts.

In general, Kane isn't too worried about how Crystal Lake tweaks or outright changes the existing Friday the 13th canon. He calls out our modern obsession with lore as completely missing the point of these movies, which conveniently gives him a lot more freedom to tell whatever story he wants. Still, maybe Kane has a point.

"I bemoan a little bit like this thing that we've gotten into," he says. "I grew up watching these movies in theaters and what they were about was sensation. They're about a collective experience, a cathartic experience, with an audience full of people. It's about taking a ride.

"But somewhere over the last 20 years, watching these slasher movies that had multiple sequels became about collecting and hoarding information. I come to these movies for character, for sensation, for the kills."

Kane isn't wrong. The Friday the 13th continuity has always been murky, at best, and the less time spent trying to apply logic to its timeline the better. That said, there are some very specific reveals in Crystal Lake's seventh episode, in particular, that I want to get into with the showrunner, and that means unpacking both how they interact with the broader Jason Voorhees lore and what they represent on this particular show.
Thankfully, Kane was happy to get into those details with me, but not before delivering one more disclaimer.
"I am the original fan of these movies," he says. "I didn't make these changes out of whole cloth or because I don't have a respect for the franchise. They came from a very specific place."
There are major spoilers for all of Crystal Lake in this article.
Jason Voorhees' new origin story, explained

After the first trailer for Crystal Lake revealed a mysterious laboratory door labeled “Argonaut,” franchise fans began to speculate that Jason was actually some sort of MKUltra-style government experiment. In response, Kane posted a picture of Arnold Schwarzenegger as Mister Freeze on Instagram with the caption: "Everybody Chill!"
The Sept. 14 post went on to shoot down most of those rumors, and suggest a few others instead:

"It’s not the CIA. He’s not a gov’t super soldier or an Eleven. He’s probably just a Chud. Or at worst a Trog. In any case, all will be known Oct. 15. Y’know, they called Copernicus a heretic at first, too. And look how that turned out!"
Turns out, Kane wasn't being entirely honest.

Crystal Lake episode 7 is essentially one extended flashback revealing how Pamela gave birth to Jason, and how he became the subject of a nefarious corporate experiment designed to create humans that could survive a nuclear blast. (This all takes place during the height of the Cold War and the era of mutually assured destruction.) Not only is Jason invulnerable, but physical trauma actually makes him grow larger and stronger at an accelerated rate.

With a wide variety of influences ranging from David Cronenberg and Rosemary's Baby to the 1950s melodramas of Douglas Sirk, there's a lot to take in throughout episode 7 — and a lot that may leave audiences with even more questions than before.

The episode opens on a young, pregnant Pamela just as she experiences a miscarriage — or so the doctor tells her. A second opinion, secured by the father (Hamish Linklater) through his sales job at a large conglomerate, reveals that the fetus is still alive, but just barely. So Pamela signs up for an experimental treatment to save the baby, which involves moving from New York to a suburban town in Texas controlled by the company.

Pamela gives birth successfully, years go by, and Jason spends a lot of time undergoing various treatments at the laboratory. Eventually, Pamela discovers the truth and finds her boy chained up in a secret facility. So she murders the doctor and flees from her husband, who has been directly involved in the experiments.
So is Jason a supersoldier? Not exactly, but he's not just a regular kid either. For Kane, the big distinction comes down to one specific detail.
"He's not a science experiment," the showrunner says. "He was a real baby who was holding on for dear life inside Pam."
Jason's new origin story is also deeply personal for Kane.

"Anybody who's ever gone through those fertility issues, which my wife and I have, knows you get to a very desperate place where you're like, 'This is a child and it's probably going to miscarry unless I take something to strengthen the follicles.'"
However, he also adds that this episode is rooted in the real history of the Cold War era.

"These experiments were going on at the time," Kane says. "Whether we're talking about things like thalidomide, or other drugs that companies were working on for very specific purposes that ultimately showed they had other properties that were useful, and so they tilted into corporate and government contracts. It seemed realistic to me that this could happen."
That other Pamela Voorhees twist

The question of why Pamela became a serial killer has always lingered in horror fans' minds, thanks in part to original actor Betsy Palmer's eerie delivery of her infamous line, "Kill her, mommy!" Those three words suggested that either Jason was possessing his mother from beyond the grave, or that her grief had completely pushed her over the edge.

Audiences have debated the question for decades, but Crystal Lake seems to provide the answer. After an incident early in episode 7 where an exhausted Pamela almost drowns her infant son (his miraculous survival is the first hint of his powers), the same doctor treating Jason prescribes Pamela some powerful antidepressants to calm her down.

Later, when Pamela rescues Jason from the lab, the doctor warns her that she's become dependent on those drugs. If she runs away, the withdrawal could permanently damage her brain. She takes the risk, but throughout Crystal Lake, it's clear that Pamela isn't just grieving her son, she's also dealing with a serious mental health disorder.

"Obviously there's the grief aspect of it," Kane says. "That's real, and that plays into the changing of her brain chemistry. But if you know anybody who's been on SSRIs or various other things and goes off cold turkey — it really changes your brain chemistry."
The show never specifies exactly what medication Pamela was taking, but the showrunner notes that the 1960s was a "much more experimental" time in that respect.
"God knows what she was on to keep her stable and quiet and gaslit while they were doing whatever they were doing to her son," he says.
For Kane, these few lines of dialogue are crucial to our entire understanding of Pamela's character, and of Crystal Lake in general.

"We wanted to explain her protectiveness with Jason," he says. "We wanted to explain how the grief could stay with her for as long as it does. And we wanted to explain how her brain chemistry could have changed to the extent that the madness would ultimately fully take hold of her, and she would become the woman that we know from the first movie."
In that sense, Crystal Lake puts an interesting new spin on Pamela Voorhees, though in the process, it arguably undercuts one of the best moments in horror movie history.
"Maybe it's a little too much explanation," Kane says, "but too fucking bad."
Crystal Lake is streaming now on Peacock.

articles.headline: The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on most of Microsoft's promises
keyFacts: Microsoft released the Surface Laptop Ultra, featuring the Nvidia RTX Spark platform to target high-performance buyers.
The laptop starts at $2,599 and reaches up to $5,899 depending on selected processor and memory configurations.
Review testing revealed some early software and hardware incompatibilities, including AI benchmarks and apps defaulting to CPU processing.
body: Over the past week, the laptop Microsoft sent me has been summarizing books and movies, generating images from my imagination, and running a 70-billion-parameter AI model that would be a stretch to fit on most laptops. It also played AAA games at a speed and fidelity I would have thought impossible on an ARM system just a year ago. Microsoft wants to sell you one computer for all of your needs, and for once that doesn’t feel like total marketing fluff. Mostly.

Microsoft is throwing both arms around the new Nvidia RTX Spark platform with the Surface Laptop Ultra—and setting its sights on the would-be MacBook Pro buyer, or as the company called it, “a high performance audience.” The bet is that rather than a gaming desktop for fun and a development laptop for work, buyers will pay more for one machine that does both.

The Surface Laptop Ultra arrives at a strange time in personal computing. Recent industry numbers showed a 20 percent drop in total PC shipments year over year in the third quarter of 2026. That’s not just consumer purchasing either—that’s across the board. Between the RAMpocalypse that has exploded consumer prices and an industry fixated on enterprise money, there hasn’t been much new hardware to excite PC enthusiasts.

Microsoft isn’t the only one debuting an RTX-chipped laptop. Dell’s XPS 16 Creator Edition and Asus’s ProArt series (our own Ryan Whitwam‘s review should be appearing on the front page soon) are betting on the chipset as well. The question when reviewing the Surface Laptop Ultra isn’t whether it can achieve the things that it claims competently, but whether there’s finally a compelling reason for power users to switch to an ARM system, and whether their daily workloads can still be achieved without hiccups when compared to a more traditional x86 offering, or the biggest competitor within the segment, the MacBook Pro.

With a starting price of $2,599, this is not a budget alternative to Apple silicon. This is bleeding-edge hardware, and you’re going to be paying a premium for it. Depending on your selected processor and memory options, MSRP can reach as high as $5,899. Prospective buyers should note that the lower-specced 24GB unified memory model ships with Windows 11 Home, while the rest of the fleet arrives with Windows 11 Pro. I received the 64GB model for testing, and I think that would probably be the sweet spot for a lot of users to align cost and performance.

I really have to wonder if 24GB is enough to go around when we know that Windows 11 is memory-hungry on its own. When you have to assign a significant portion of that 24GB of unified memory to VRAM for gaming, does performance suffer? An audience question inside the Surface Laptop Ultra review information session asked about the usefulness of the base model, and didn’t get much back other than a vague “useful for smaller models locally” answer. Microsoft may have a more definitive answer to that question a few months from now when software and drivers catch up with hardware.
So has the Microsoft and Nvidia team-up created the ultimate all-in-one laptop? Or is this the industry once again putting the hardware hype cart before the finished-software horse?
Surface Laptop Ultra specs
Display

The 15-inch mini-LED display might not be enough to get folks to run to the Ultra on its own, but it’s a compelling reason to add it to the list. The 3270×2180 native resolution looks simply stunning whether you’re watching a 4K video, playing games, or just staring at a desktop spreadsheet. I preferred the Enhanced color profile, but Vivid and sRGB modes looked fantastic as well.

Blacks stayed deep against bright, vivid subjects without any sort of visible blooming. I wish I could say the same for my TV. While I can’t quantify how it stacks side by side with the latest MacBook Pro Retina display, I can say that this is a damn nice screen. Viewing angles are superb, colors are punchy, and the 2,000-nit peak brightness kept things legible even in a room flooded with natural sunlight. My only gripe is that in bright rooms, there is glare to contend with. The glossy glass looks fantastic at lower light levels but can act a bit mirror-like in direct sunlight. It hindered my ability to photograph the screen more than it did my ability to use the computer. Still, if you’re looking for a matte-screen laptop, you might want to keep that in mind.
Keyboard and trackpad

The keyboard on the Surface Laptop Ultra is exactly what you’d expect on a premium machine like this. It’s excellent, if unremarkable. The keys have a shallow but satisfying press, the spacing makes sense for my hands, and the whole package delivers a very comfortable typing experience. I don’t have a whole bunch of laptops lying around to compare it to, but unsurprisingly, the closest would be my 2020 MacBook Pro. Microsoft knows what market it’s going after here, and I don’t mind them lifting direct inspiration from Apple in this department.

The trackpad is similarly competent. It’s absolutely huge, measuring 5.5 inches long by 3.5 inches tall, with excellent tracking accuracy throughout my testing time. Normally, one of the first things I do when plugging in a laptop to work from is to attach an external mouse, but over days of testing, I never reached for the mouse drawer. Microsoft made a point to emphasize the trackpad’s haptic feedback capabilities in native programs during the review information session. I’m not sure if there are still updates left to come that I haven’t received yet, but I can’t recall a time when I noticed additional mouse haptics had kicked in when I opened MS Office or anything. As it stands, the trackpad isn’t groundbreaking, but it is premium enough to be part of an “ultra” laptop.
Magnetic USB-C charging

Microsoft describes the included magnetic charging connection and port as being “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C charging experience.” It’s difficult to get upset about the marketing department doing their jobs, but this claim struck me as more of a technical truth than engineering feat. Apple’s MagSafe charging debuted on the original MacBook Pro all the way back in 2006. The concept of a breakaway magnetic charger isn’t anything new, but technically Microsoft’s assertion holds water in that it is the first USB-C connector on a laptop with a matching magnetic port, rather than a proprietary connector.

Marketing claims aside, the magnetic connection does work well. The port and charger naturally guide themselves together, as magnets do, and made plugging the laptop in to charge in a dark room hassle-free. Normally I’d be holding the cord in one hand while trying to fumble around in the dark for the phone in my pocket and remember the gesture to quickly turn on the flashlight. Now I just have to get the cable within the vicinity, and the magnets do the rest. Perfect for when all I want to do is plug the PC in and go to bed.

What’s perhaps the larger selling point for magnetic charging is the cable’s ability to break away if yanked from the PC. Nothing will ruin your day faster than watching a new laptop fly off the counter. With the breakaway cable, you’re getting peace of mind that your laptop shouldn’t meet the floor should a startled cat or curious toddler come into contact with the cable. I’ve never had it happen with one of my laptops, but that doesn’t mean accidents don’t occur. I simulated a few ‘accidental disconnects’ with modest force, and the cable disconnected dutifully as it should.

While I won’t say that it’s a must-have, it’s certainly a nice-to-have. And in this package it’s certainly the type of premium accessory you’d expect, but it’s not going to move units on its own—not at these price tiers.
Geekbench

According to Nvidia, the RTX Spark N1X is a Grace CPU fused to a Blackwell GPU. Unlike chipsets like AMD’s Ryzen AI and Intel’s Core Ultra series, the N1X has no dedicated NPU—instead it leans on unified memory and the heavy-duty Blackwell GPU for AI work. Traditionally, Copilot+ certification has hinged on a 40+ TOPS NPU, but Microsoft is extending the label to this machine’s GPU-based AI performance anyway (more on that later).

The graphics bench tests sing when given access to 40GB+ of usable RAM. These results certainly back up Microsoft’s claims that the Surface Laptop Ultra can handle modern AAA gaming. It just takes some different paths to performance than we might be used to.

The AI benchmark was a bit of a miss. I don’t have the ability to run an NPU-accelerated benchmark in Geekbench AI, because the software presumably doesn’t currently have a compatible NPU backend for this unique architecture. Curiously, Windows does list a generic NPU under Display Adapters in Device Manager, but Geekbench AI only offered the ONNX CPU testing path. It’s unclear whether the generic NPU listed by Windows is a virtual device, some sort of driver exposure, or something else entirely.

It isn’t possible to get performance metrics on hardware that Geekbench can’t properly see yet. It’s still early days, but it’s the kind of software/hardware incompatibility that you hate to run into when just trying to check out what your new computer can do. The CPU score in Geekbench AI isn’t particularly impressive, and bypassing the Blackwell sort of defeats the purpose of this hardware, so I hope that as the RTX Spark devices start getting out there, we’ll be able to get a better idea of the full potential.
AI testing was limited to the CPU for now.
AI testing was limited to the CPU for now.
AI testing was limited to the CPU for now.
AI testing (where possible) with AI Dev Gallery

Microsoft recommended reviewers try its new AI Dev Gallery app (preview) as a way to test on-device AI. The software is currently in public preview, and users can pull models of their choice directly from Hugging Face for testing or workflow. The project’s GitHub carries a helpful word of warning about running models on ARM64-based Copilot+ PCs, which, according to Microsoft, this is. Or will be, eventually. Confusing, isn’t it?

⚠️ Note: On ARM64-based Copilot+ PCs, make sure to build and run the solution as ARM64 (and not as x64). This is required, especially when running the samples that communicate with models such as Phi Silica.

On paper, AI Dev Gallery should have been a simple one-stop shop to test a barrage of different models against the Surface Laptop Ultra’s new RTX Spark setup. In practice, all of the available conversational Phi and Mistral models in the app are CPU-only—no GPU or NPU pathways available, despite the Blackwell sitting there idling. GPU and NPU paths are available for some image generation and embedded model options, but it again leaves me with that lingering feeling that we’re pushing cutting edge hardware just to have something to offer the market. Oh, and it’s worth noting that twice during my testing, I was browsing AI Dev Gallery’s model selection when the program abruptly froze and then crashed entirely back to desktop. There are still rough edges to smooth out.

Phi Silica, Microsoft’s flagship on-device LLM and a major piece of the Copilot+ stack, cannot be accessed out of the gate. Accessing the API requires a developer registration with an associated app identity. These may seem like obvious steps for those already in the AI-know, but curious consumers might get frustrated by reaching a gate in what is advertised as a ready-to-run experience out of the box.

AI Dev Gallery conversational model (Mistral 7B Instruct 0.2 CPU) — Cutting out the GPU, this CPU-only model was still able to manage about 11 tokens/sec. Slower than a GPU path for sure, but it’s interesting that the CPU alone can manage smaller models at a reasonable conversation rate.

AI Dev Gallery image generation(Stable Diffusion v1.4) — I attempted image generation harnessing the CPU by accident at first. That didn’t fare so well, but as soon as I switched over to the NvTensorRT (GPU) option, I was able to generate images from a prompt in about three to four seconds by my stopwatch. The results aren’t the best you’ve ever seen, but with additional prompting and image coaxing, I’m confident that they could have been improved. Whether you need local AI image generation on your daily driver is another matter.

I attempted to follow Microsoft’s instructions listed in the AI Dev Gallery to run a CUDA-accelerated Phi model, but the process failed. After resolving some command-line issues, pip downloaded the correct Python 3.13 package of onnxruntime-genai-cuda for Windows ARM64, but then failed because the required onnxruntime-gpu dependency doesn’t seem to have a compatible distribution for this environment. Logs indicated the CUDA install path wasn’t usable on this setup at this time. Whether this is a limitation of the current package, an ARM64 packaging gap, or human error, I can’t be totally sure. It was just frustrating to feel so limited in the space where Microsoft told me to play.
I attempt to prompt my way into a picture of my dog.
I attempt to prompt my way into a picture of my dog.
The results of my watercolor cat prompt.
The results of my watercolor cat prompt.
AI’s image prompt interpretation of a monster of a unicycle.
AI’s image prompt interpretation of a monster of a unicycle.
The results of my watercolor cat prompt.
AI’s image prompt interpretation of a monster of a unicycle.
Ollama

Frustrated with the current state of Microsoft’s AI Dev Gallery app, I decided to try some testing via Ollama running locally in the command prompt. I downloaded the Llama3.3-70b model. That’s a 43GB model—10 times the size of the Mistral model we ran on the CPU in AI Dev Gallery, with 10 times the parameters (70 billion over 7).

If I were Microsoft, this is the type of demo I’d want to be showing off. This massive 70B model would be unlikely to run on any discrete laptop GPU, but the Blackwell still managed 6.26 tokens/sec. The fact that it ran at all is impressive, though I will say this was one of the few times when the Blackwell really seemed to be sweating. System fans were spinning at 100 percent while those Wayne’s World synopses were being written. Credit where due, even at full tilt, the fans don’t generate a lot of sound other than the high-speed pushing of air.
Gaming

When Microsoft speaks of a high performance audience, none is more demanding than the modern high-end PC gamer. I’m old enough that I still find 1080p/60 Hz gaming to look great, and that’s probably for the best, given the current cost of video cards, but those who crave the zero input lag, 4K, ray-traced life are a particular bunch. Whether the package on offer with the Surface Laptop Ultra will be high performance enough for that audience will be up to the individual gamer and their wallet, but this gamer was certainly impressed that these results were coming out of an ARM machine.

Microsoft claims 85 percent of its Game Pass library is currently playable on ARM, but I had difficulty trying to find if any titles have a native ARM port, or if they were running in x64 through the Prism lens of emulation. Windows Performance Fit offers a glimpse into how the game might perform on your system, but nothing more. Either way, if it’s the playing of games that you’re concerned with, there shouldn’t be much this system won’t run. The full Nvidia DLSS feature set seems to be available, and ray tracing boxes can be clicked in graphics options. Factor in an HDR-capable display, and the Surface Laptop Ultra is covering a lot of the must-haves for modern gamers.

After an initial boot of Gears of War: E-Day that saw a solid 4–5 minutes of shader compiling, I was concerned that this might be an every-time occurrence, but subsequent loads were much faster. This is a game that contains anti-cheat, the latest Unreal Engine, and all the imaginable graphical bells and whistles you’d want from one of your company’s prized franchises. It’s here and running quite well on the Surface Laptop Ultra. While benchmarking, I noticed the system had reported an astonishing 46.7GiB of its 64GiB of unified memory as available VRAM for the game.

To their credit, Microsoft has included a warning for consumers who might not be familiar with the new Surface Laptop Ultra architecture: “App compatibility: Surface Laptop Ultra runs Windows 11 on an Arm-based Nvidia RTX Spark platform. Many popular apps run natively on Arm. Apps that are not built for Arm can run through Prism, Windows’ built-in emulator. If you rely on specialized hardware drivers, plug-ins, or older utilities, check app and driver compatibility before purchase.”

Multiplayer titles with kernel-level anti-cheat measures may fail or show warnings under Prism emulation due to signature mismatches in system files. Each time I ran Gears of War: E-Day, I was greeted with a warning message when exiting back into Windows. It appears as though the Easy Anti-Cheat was flagging the .NET cache as “modified,” though I couldn’t establish whether Prism’s translation was directly responsible.
Additional benchmark results in Forza Horizon 6.
Additional benchmark results in Forza Horizon 6.
Graphics settings in Forza Horizon 6.
Graphics settings in Forza Horizon 6.
Graphics settings in Forza Horizon 6.
An impressive pool of available memory.
HandBrake

Beyond gaming, I wanted to see how video encoding would fare on the new hardware. I ran a real-world encode test via HandBrake on the 2160p 60 fps version of the famous Big Buck Bunny. The system processed the 10-minute video clip in 2:27 at 180 fps using x264 encoding via the CPU. That’s the snag. Nvidia NVENC or Nvidia HEVC encoding options are nowhere to be found, meaning the Blackwell’s encode engine still isn’t being exposed to the software. That’s not a problem with HandBrake, it’s just the continuation of a familiar pattern. Hardware decode worked just fine via Media Foundation, so it’s specifically the encode side of things running into a roadblock.
Copilot+

According to Microsoft in the review information session I attended, the Surface Laptop Ultra will be certified as a Copilot+ device, but “full software support won’t arrive until late 2026 or early 2027.” The keyboard’s dedicated Copilot button launches the window for M365 Copilot right now, which is fine if you intended to use it for Cloud AI services, but users may be confused at first given the package they were sold.

Features like Recall, Click to Do, and the new Windows search bar won’t be available until Microsoft finishes baking them for the Surface Laptop Ultra’s hardware. Participants in the Windows Insider Program will likely see early access before the general public, so if you’re itching for those Copilot+ features, you’ll have to agree to participate and share device information with Microsoft. Your call.
Unscientific battery testing

Since the Surface Laptop Ultra is meant to be an all-day device that can handle your workload during the day and your gaming at night, there’s an unavoidable question of how much of that you can actually do on the go. With this in mind, I attempted to measure battery levels every 30 minutes throughout my testing and mapped it to a partial day of mixed use.

The Surface retained 66 percent of battery life after three hours of varied use. AI-heavy application use will have you running for the magnetic plug, though. That final 30-minute sample was when I ran the llama3.3:70b model twice, and there was a significant drop-off during that period that would likely remain constant so long as you were pushing the GPU.
Sound

Speakers on the Surface Laptop Ultra are impressive for such a slim device. I unwittingly found myself sitting at my desk bobbing my head along to the Forza Horizon 6 theme music while benchmarks were running. To no real surprise given the size constraints, it’s the low-end frequencies that seem most absent in the overall sound, but that’s not to say there’s anything hollow about the final mix.

The package is quite serviceable given that most people are going to be using headphones with the device in an office setting or on the go. I didn’t do any dB measuring, but cranking the volume in my basement was loud enough to get my wife to ask what the heck I was doing from the floor above. Normally it takes reference speakers for that reaction, so I’ll call them sufficiently loud. At no point did I encounter any type of crackles or pops when adjusting volume on the fly, which is always a nice sign that everything is shielded as it should be.
Closing thoughts

The Surface Laptop Ultra is a very capable machine, perhaps even more capable in places than I had assumed. Through clever resource allocations via unified memory and the new RTX Spark SoC, Microsoft has genuinely delivered on the hardware side of its “one device for everything” pitch. When a 70 billion-parameter model can run on this laptop with GPU acceleration and not others, that’s impressive. The Surface Laptop Ultra delivers on the gaming portion of its promises, too: AAA titles running on an ARM machine, complete with the latest bells and whistles, and displayed on one of the nicest laptop displays I’ve ever seen. From the screen to the keyboard to the trackpad, everything feels premium, because it is.

The problem isn’t the laptop’s hardware, but everything currently sitting on top of it. Microsoft’s own AI Dev Gallery still feels half-baked, with a limited selection of small models mostly tied to the CPU. Phi Silica, the flagship LLM, is still gated behind developer registration. The Copilot+ features are still to come at a later date, which might be this year or next. None of these are fatal flaws on their own; this thing is still prelaunch at the time of writing after all. But taken as a whole, you start to see a pattern. PCs are being rushed to market with the new RTX Spark chipset so that manufacturers at least have something new to offer for the 2026 holiday season, with software left to play catch-up later on some non-specific date.

So who is the Surface Laptop Ultra really for? If you’re a CUDA developer who favors portability and needs to test local AI models on the fly, and you happen to have an extra $2,599–$5,899 in your back pocket, this is genuinely exciting hardware. For everyone else? I’d advise patience. Take a pause to see how the software matures before jumping ship from your MacBook Pro.

There’s also an element of PC philosophy to consider. I’m the type of person who enjoys purpose-built systems for specific tasks. A desktop rig for gaming, a mini-PC for office work, a laptop or Chromebook for cloud applications on the road. It’s just how I’ve become wired. “This is my PC for that,” as it were. Though with PC prices likely to stay inflated for at least another few years, maybe Microsoft and Nvidia have delivered a middle ground.

If you’re the type of person who really does want everything in one package, then the Surface Laptop Ultra’s multiple personalities may actually suit you. But the math is still somewhat complicated. You’re paying a premium for bleeding-edge tech where not all features are available yet, and having to do so under the umbrella of Microsoft services, with all the live logins and subscriptions that come with it.
The good, the bad, and the ugly
The good:
One of the nicest laptop displays you’re likely to see
Premium hardware and design
Gaming runs shockingly well on ARM
Serious CUDA compute performance on a laptop
Magnetic USB-C charging is a nice touch
Unified memory
The bad:
Copilot+ features are still several months away
AI Dev Gallery’s Preview is still light on features to take advantage of this hardware
Expensive silicon shipping without full driver support
The ugly:
Software support just isn’t there quite yet

Has Microsoft and Nvidia’s partnership delivered the ultimate all-in-one PC? Not yet, but they have delivered the first ARM laptop I’ve used that makes the question worth asking—now the horse just needs to show up.

Nick Indge is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica covering hardware, embedded systems, and self-hosted infrastructure. A former security investigator turned tech writer, he writes to help readers escape subscription traps and regain ownership of their digital lives. He lives in Chicagoland with his family and a goofball husky.

articles.headline: NYPD Commish Jessica Tisch roasts Mamdani, jokes about far left’s demands to fire her at Al Smith Dinner
keyFacts: NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch joked about far-left demands for her removal and her relationship with Mayor Zohran Mamdani during the Al Smith Dinner.
Tisch received the Happy Warrior Award at the annual charity event hosted by the Archdiocese of New York.
Tisch and the NYPD recently faced criticism from allies of the mayor following the police department's response to anti-ICE protests.
body: NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch showed off her sense of humor at Thursday night’s Al Smith Dinner — leaving New York’s great and good in stitches with a series of well-timed cracks about far-left demands that Mayor Zohran Mamdani remove her as NYC’s top cop.

“There’s a lot of talk these days that the mayor’s friends don’t like me,” Tisch set up an audience that included Hizzoner before zinging: “That’s simply not true – President Trump and I get along great!“
The commissioner briefly turned serious by acknowledging that “things got a little hot for me this week” before asking the high-rolling audience: “Just in case, anybody hiring?”

Elsewhere in her remarks, the third-generation member of the Loews Corporation dynasty claimed that Mamdani had told her last year he was keeping her on as boss of the boys and girls in blue because “Jessie, I ran on taxing the rich, you’re going to need a job.”

Tisch, 45, was honored with the Happy Warrior Award at the annual dinner hosted by the Archdiocese of New York, renowned as a chance for politicians to take off their partisan armor and rib each other in the name of supporting the city’s needy.

“This dinner is an opportunity to set aside our religious and political differences,” she said. “Which is wonderful, because I’m a Jewish police commissioner working for a Muslim mayor, and tonight I’m being honored by the Catholic Church. God Bless America.”

“It’s been delightful sitting next to you today at this dinner,” Archbishop Ronald Hicks, presiding over his first Al Smith Dinner, told Tisch in presenting the award. “You are our Happy Warrior. And I just want to thank you, and also to thank your true service of continuing your family’s legacy of public service. Thank you.”

Hicks’ precedessor, Timothy Cardinal Dolan, thanked the commissioner — whom he referred to as “Wonder Woman” — for giving him the opportunity to serve as NYPD co-chief chaplain and said she was doing “a splendid job.”

Lynda Carter, the actress who originated the “Wonder Woman” role on the classic 1970s TV show, was also among the attendees — but not even the DC Comics heroine’s famous Lasso of Truth could get a word out of Mamdani, who did not address the gathering and whose office had no immediate comment on Tisch’s jokes.

Tisch and the NYPD came under fire following the department’s response to anti-ICE protests that broke out over the Oct. 8 shooting by federal agents of illegal migrant and suspected gang member Oscar Belgal in the Marble Hill section of The Bronx.

Allies of Mamdani, like soon-to-be congresswoman Darializa Avila Chevalier, have called for Tisch to step down or be removed as well as for the disbanding of the NYPD’s elite Strategic Response Group — wrongly accusing cops of violating NYC’s sanctuary city laws that bar officers from assisting ICE.

articles.headline: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost
keyFacts: The Center for AI Safety maintains a Wage Loss Dashboard that estimates national and state-level wage losses resulting from AI-attributed job cuts.
The dashboard reported over 117,000 job cuts attributed to AI nationally in 2026, resulting in an estimated $8.5 billion in annual wage losses.
Researchers noted that the dashboard estimates state impacts by applying national shares of AI-cited cuts to announced state job cuts rather than tracking observed layoffs directly.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- AI-related job losses impact local community economics.
- The CAIS tracker puts these losses in dollars and cents.
- Understanding how AI will change the economy still involves guesswork.

Fears of how AI will impact the economy and job availability are running rampant after a few years of steady layoffs at major companies. Much of that fear can be attributed to labs and CEOs juicing their own relevance, but some job cuts have been explicitly tied to AI’s rapid acceleration.
The Center for AI Safety (CAIS) maintains a tracker that keeps tabs on how these changes are impacting family wages.
Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires
More from ZDNET

The Wage Loss Dashboard includes a map of where layoffs have occurred since January 2026 (it was just updated this month to include September data) and a drop-down that shows data for the entire country or an individual state. As of now, the dashboard finds just over 117,000 job cuts attributed to AI nationally this year — $8.5 billion in estimated annual wage losses.

The Wage Loss Dashboard multiplies the number of AI-attributed job cuts by the average annual salary to estimate annual wage loss. According to the dashboard, wage estimates “begin to show what those cuts can mean for households and local economies.”

The dashboard also displays the estimated average wage loss per person based on that layoff data, presented relative to everyday expenses, like a tank of gas. For the country as a whole, it’s $25 per person per year. Not much, but the numbers shift by state: In California, for example, it’s $56. That’s thanks to a much higher concentration of job cuts (just over 27,000 layoffs attributed to AI). Alaska, on the other hand, claims only 138 job losses ($14 per person).

Those aren’t the exact numbers of people laid off for AI in California and Alaska this year, however. As CAIS explains, “The dashboard estimates AI-attributed cuts for each state, converts them to estimated annual wage loss, then divides by state population to estimate the average loss per person. State estimates are not observed AI layoffs. We apply each month’s national share of cuts citing AI to that state’s announced job cuts.”
From layoffs to dollars and cents

The dashboard uses a few sources of data: monthly reporting from Challenger, Gray, and Christmas, which compiles layoff announcements from across the US by state as well as national job cuts credited to AI, and data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on every state’s annual mean wage. CAIS also refers to population estimates from the US Census Bureau.
Also: 3 ways AI can help you ace your next job interview

In 2025, the Challenger, Gray, and Christmas reports identified over 54,000 job cuts that companies publicly linked to AI. That translates to one in 20 layoffs from last year. But tracking job losses alone is a more abstract metric than what those layoffs mean in monetary terms to the people experiencing them.

“There has been significant news coverage of job loss from AI, but it can be hard to quantify how these cuts affect the average person’s finances,” CAIS wrote of the project. “This dashboard aims to help illuminate the monetary costs of AI on American families and communities.”
As CAIS points out, the impact of layoffs shows up in ripples across grocery stores, small businesses, rent, and other local costs.

“One person’s layoff means less income for every business they support. Multiply that effect across thousands of workers in multiple industries, and you start to see the real economic weight of AI displacement,” the researchers behind the project wrote. “In addition, AI-attributed job cuts aren’t spread evenly. States with large tech and media sectors are experiencing greater impact.”

A few caveats: CAIS noted that this dashboard doesn’t include “jobs created by AI, productivity gains, re-employment, or secondary economic effects.” That’s partly because experts don’t have a consensus on whether or how much AI will stimulate the economy or outpace job displacement. AI-attributed layoffs are themselves murky: The data here are job cuts companies themselves said were tied to AI. Without a single definition for what that means or complete transparency from companies, it’s not always 100% provable that a layoff was the direct result of obsolescence or replacement spurred by AI.
Also: Companies embracing AI the most are hiring more people

“We don’t require an executive to say ‘we replaced a team with AI.’ This is a moderate standard, deliberately: it captures the broad pattern of AI-justified workforce reductions while excluding clearly unrelated cuts,” the Alliance for Secure AI wrote of its methodology.

Other trackers like Jobloss.ai, which is run by the Alliance for Secure AI, also catalog job loss data by company, date, and how explicitly companies cited AI around those layoffs. Because of how amorphous these data can be to track, Jobloss.ai only logs layoffs that meet certain criteria: at least 100 jobs in one fell swoop, accompanied by some mention of AI (or proxy terms, like “automation” and “productivity”).
The dashboard aims to make the data we do have more accessible — not to shame any particular industry or company for its AI adoption choices.

“AI is a technology being adopted by companies for many reasons,” CAIS wrote. “Our goal is to make the costs of that adoption visible, so workers, communities, and policymakers can respond with real information instead of guesses.”
Automating remote labor

The Wage Loss Dashboard also includes a section on how well AI is completing remote freelance tasks. Using data from the Remote Labor Index (RLI) benchmark CAIS co-developed, which tests agents on real-world freelance tasks like web development and video production, CAIS shows how quickly agents are evolving.

“When RLI launched, the best AI agent completed just 2.5% of projects at professional quality. Eight months later, that number has risen to 15.8%,” researchers wrote. As of now, AI can fully automate almost 16% of remote tasks, a percentage that’s doubling every 3.7 months. Claude Fable 5 comes in on top, followed by OpenAI’s GPT-5.5.

But that doesn’t mean AI is gobbling up those projects from human freelancers. RLI measures what AI models are capable of doing, not what they’re actively taking on. That said, CAIS maintains alarm about what it sees as a trend: the convergence of AI-attributed job cuts with increasingly work-capable agents.

While legislation can’t explicitly prevent companies from opting for AI systems over hiring humans in certain cases, recent laws in a few states, including the tech-sector-heavy state of California, aim to make sure firing and other disciplinary decisions aren’t completely automated by AI systems.

articles.headline: How to complete A 3-Course Halloween Meal! in Disney Dreamlight Valley
keyFacts: Players must eat Green Candy, Purple Candy, and Red Candy to complete the A 3-Course Halloween Meal! duty in Disney Dreamlight Valley.
Candy can be earned by finding Halloween Buckets in the Plaza biome or by going trick-or-treating at participating villager homes.
Finishing the duty unlocks the Green Trick-or-Treater's Bounty furniture item as a reward.
body: Disney Dreamlight Valley’s Trick-or-Treat event is a massive annual festivity, with loads to get done throughout to earn all kinds of exclusive rewards. One of the many missions you’ll face in this event is the A 3-Course Halloween Meal! duty.

The tough part of this event is that all the quests included in it give you no guidance outside of the name for each one. It’s all up to you to figure out what’s being asked of you, so if this one has you stumped, here’s how to complete A 3-Course Halloween Meal! in Disney Dreamlight Valley .

A 3-Course Halloween Meal! duty reward in Disney Dreamlight Valley
A 3-Course Halloween Meal! duty in Disney Dreamlight Valley

There are a couple of different ways you can earn event Candy for Trick-or-Treat:

Find and open Halloween Buckets. For the duration of the event, you can find sparkling green, orange, and purple buckets around the Plaza biome. The green ones give you Green Candy, the orange ones give you Red Candy, and the purple ones give you Purple Candy. Carefully scour the Plaza biome consistently to stock up on Candy you can consume for the 3-Course Halloween Meal! duty.
